French cloud operator OVHcloud jumped 18 per cent to a near one-month high after reporting its first positive levered free cash flow since its 2021 listing.

Comet Holding jumped 4.7 per cent following an increase in the electronic equipment maker’s third-quarter sales due to expansion of data centres and AI ‌infrastructure.

Schneider Electric fell 3.3 per cent after ⁠the French electrical equipment maker raised €6 billion in an accelerated bookbuild, a fast share sale to institutional investors.

London

Britain’s FTSE 100 ended lower ‌on Tuesday as banks and commodity-linked stocks weighed, while signs of resilience in the labour market kept expectations ‌alive for a Bank of England rate hike next month.

The blue-chip FTSE 100 index fell 0.29 per cent to ​10,733.00 points, while the midcap FTSE 250 was down 0.06 per cent at 24,364.

Banks eased 0.8 per cent and hit a more than four-month low. Heavyweight lenders HSBC, Lloyds and NatWest fell between 0.8 per cent ⁠and 1.2 per cent.

Energy stocks ​also weighed on the market, with heavyweights BP ​and Shell down 1.7 per cent and 0.7 per cent, respectively

The FTSE 350 basic resources index was ‌down 1.6 per cent, with miner Anglo American ​falling 2 per cent after maintaining its 2026 copper production guidance despite a 5 per cent drop in ⁠third-quarter copper output.

Technology and online grocery firm Ocado rose 6.6 per cent to top the FTSE 250 after JP Morgan raised its price target on the stock to 460 pence from 290 pence.

New York

Wall Street’s main indexes moved higher on Tuesday as ‌a surge in healthcare stocks and softer oil prices boosted risk appetite, building on a recovery from last week’s technology-led sell-off.

Brent crude prices slipped 1.1 per cent after touching a ​five-month high in a choppy session as traders weighed Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure and reports of vessel attacks in the Gulf.

Most S&P 500 sectors gained, with healthcare hitting an all-time high. The gains were led by large-cap drugmakers, including Eli Lilly’s 4.7 per cent jump to a record high. Amgen, Pfizer, Johnson & Johnson and AbbVie were also up ​more than 2 per cent each.

The financial index also gained 1.2 per cent.

Energy, however, led the losses, while an about 2 per cent decline in Meta Platforms pulled the communication services sector down.

The market extended ⁠Monday’s rebound, as investors bought the dip in technology stocks following last week’s bruising sell-off, fuelled in part by concerns over ‌CoreWeave’s debt ‌load ​and the cost of financing the AI buildout.

AI-related shares were flat to higher on Tuesday, after early weakness in premarket trading. CoreWeave was last up 2.5 per cent, while the chip gauge Philadelphia Semiconductor index rose 0.7 per cent.

“You’re seeing ⁠some strength in some high-value stocks and the Dow, ​and so that’s helping to sort of lift the overall indexes,” said ​Robert Pavlik, senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth. – Additional reporting by Reuters

]]>Christophe Ena<![CDATA[Aviation firm co-founder ousted during sick leave wins €41,000 for unfair dismissal at WRC]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/aviation-firm-founder-ousted-during-sick-leave-wins-41000-for-unfair-dismissal-at-wrc/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/aviation-firm-founder-ousted-during-sick-leave-wins-41000-for-unfair-dismissal-at-wrc/Tue, 20 Oct 2026 18:01:19 +0000

An aviation maintenance firm which dismissed one of its co-founders while he was out of work sick following a breakdown in relations at the firm during a €1.2 million pay dispute has been awarded €41,000 at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC).

Gerry Burke secured the award against Magellan Aviation Services Ltd on foot of a complaint under the Unfair Dismissals Act 1977, following the termination of his employment in August 2023 after 33 years at the firm.

Burke was a co-founder and managing director of the company prior to its acquisition in 2013 by the Tokyo-headquartered Marubeni Corporation, the WRC heard.

Having been paid an “eight-figure” sum for his shareholding, Burke moved to Malta for tax reasons, and stepped down as managing director to a new post as director of special projects, the company’s lawyers submitted.

His base salary in that job was €80,000 – later increased to €88,000 – with health insurance, pension contribution and a contractual provision for a €305,000-a-year bonus, bringing his total annual remuneration to €369,786, his lawyers said.

A preliminary objection by the company submitted that the Unfair Dismissals Act did not apply, arguing that Burke lived in Malta, carried out his work “entirely outside” Ireland, and had his salary paid free of Irish income tax. This argument was rejected.

The company received tax advice in 2022 that it was unlawful to pay Burke his salary without deducting either Irish or Maltese tax, it was submitted.

It sought to “regularise” the situation with a new contract increasing Burke’s pay and requiring he pay income tax in Malta, but Burke rejected this, the company submitted further.

Burke said in evidence that the allegations of “tax evasion” levelled at him by the firm were “thrown in to discredit [him] and put a cloud over his reputation”. He was “tax-compliant in Ireland and in Malta”, he said.

His position was that he had contacted Marubeni’s compliance department in 2022 with what his lawyers submitted was a protected disclosure concerning the sale of the company, management practices, and certain pay and contract matters, the tribunal was told.

It was Burke’s case that an investigation into the pay and contract matters proceeded first, with a directive issued from Marubeni that Burke receive a 15 per cent pay rise, which was not actioned, his lawyers submitted further.

The company’s managing director, Niall Duggan, said that when he put the proposal to Burke at a meeting in Zurich, the complainant “suggested that he would move to Dubai”.

Duggan added that Burke “intended to sue [the company] if it took action to ensure that it complied with [Malta’s] tax legislation”.

Burke agreed he had threatened an injunction but said that without the firm sharing its tax advice with him, he could not reasonably agree to the company’s plans to establish a company in Malta and make him an employee there.

In 2023, Duggan said, “matters became increasingly fractious”, with Burke initiating a High Court action in Ireland and seeking to escalate the dispute to the leadership of the Marubeni Corporation in Japan.

In March that year, Burke underwent “serious surgery”, his legal team submitted. The actions of Magellan caused him “stress and strain” and delayed his recovery, it was further submitted.

After about five months’ absence due to sick leave, the company terminated Burke’s employment on the basis of disability, the tribunal noted.

There was “an express contractual provision under which an executive is automatically deemed to have a disability following an extended absence from work due to ill-health” in Burke’s employment contract, the adjudication officer noted.

Although Burke sought reinstatement as his preferred remedy for the dismissal, his legal papers calculated his total losses at more than €1.2 million, the WRC recorded.

The WRC noted that Burke had alleged non-payment of salary going back to 2020, and had initiated separate proceedings in the High Court.

Ruling the dismissal unfair, adjudicator Ewa Sobanska wrote: “I cannot accept that other matters, some of them still remaining unresolved, had no impact on the respondent’s decision to dismiss [Burke], Sobanska wrote.

She was not satisfied the termination arose “wholly or mainly” due to any question of Burke’s capability, she wrote.

However, she found she could not order reinstatement on the basis of “fractious relationships” and “tension between the parties”.

Sobanska wrote that €41,434.08, about six months’ base salary, was a “just and equitable” award for the dismissal.

This was because she could not take Burke’s claimed bonus payments into account, and she regarded his efforts to seek new work to be “inadequate”.

Peter O’Brien was for the respondent, instructed by solicitor Melvyn Hanley. Ercus Stewart appeared with Tom McGowan for the complainant, instructed by Edward Kelly of Holmes O’Malley Solicitors.

]]><![CDATA[Live commerce platform Whatnot to double Irish workforce in 18 months]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/live-commerce-platform-whatnot-to-double-irish-workforce-in-18-months/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/live-commerce-platform-whatnot-to-double-irish-workforce-in-18-months/Tue, 20 Oct 2026 17:08:23 +0000Live commerce platform Whatnot is to double its Irish workforce in the next 18 months as it expands its European headquarters in Dublin.

The company is also planning to open the platform to Irish sellers in 2027.

Whatnot, which has been operating in Ireland for the past four years, currently employs 130 people. It is targeting close to 300 in the near future, with roles in engineering, artificial intelligence (AI), operations, strategy, and trust and safety being created.

The platform allows businesses and individuals to sell through live video, demonstrating products and taking orders in real time. The first half of the year saw sellers generate more than €6.8 billion in sales.

The Dublin team plays an important role in keeping the platform working, reliable and secure, working on payments, buying and selling flows and infrastructure. The expansion will see new AI engineering recruits build tools to help reduce admin tasks for sellers, from product listings to post-show tasks.

Cofounder and chief executive Grant LaFontaine said the company had been building quietly in recent years. It also has an office in Berlin, but the focus is on growing the team in Dublin.

“The vast majority of hiring is happening in Dublin, so it is the biggest office outside the US and it will be for a while,” he said.

“Six years ago we had 10 people, so to go from that to 1,400 [globally], it is quite a large sum.”

There are Irish buyers on the platform, with the number of people in Ireland shopping on Whatnot each month has grown almost fivefold over the past two years, but officially Whatnot has not opened to Irish sellers. That has left most orders filled by sellers in the UK, Germany and the US. That will change next year, with Whatnot opening to Irish businesses.

The news of the expansion was welcomed by Minister of State at Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment Alan Dillon.

“The company’s plan to double its team in Ireland, creating high-quality jobs across engineering, AI, operations, and trust and safety, is a strong endorsement of the exceptional talent available here and of Ireland’s attractiveness as a location for innovation,” he said.

IDA Ireland’s executive director Mary Buckley said the decision demonstrated strong confidence in Ireland’s technology ecosystem and skilled workforce.

]]><![CDATA[Millions affected by Revolut disruption linked to Google Cloud outage]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/revolut-services-hit-by-outage-including-in-ireland/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/revolut-services-hit-by-outage-including-in-ireland/Tue, 20 Oct 2026 16:33:03 +0000Millions of customers of digital bank Revolut found themselves unable to access financial services after a power outage at Google Cloud caused widespread disruption on Tuesday.

Customers across Ireland and the UK reported problems accessing the bank’s systems, from logging in to the app and transferring funds, to making card payments and cash withdrawals.

The disruption was linked to an outage at Google Cloud, which provides core infrastructure services to Revolut.

The problems began early on Tuesday morning and lasted for several hours, with Downdetector recording a spike in reports between 7 and 8am. Revolut confirmed the outage, but moved to reassure customers that their data and money had not been compromised.

“We are currently experiencing a service disruption affecting multiple services. We can confirm that all our customers’ money and data are safe,” a spokesman said. “We’ve been working to fix the issue since it was identified this morning and apologise to anyone affected and for any inconvenience caused.”

Revolut customers in Ireland affected by ‘third-party’ data breach

Revolut has 3.4 million customers in Ireland.

Google later confirmed the problem was caused by a “power event” at Google Cloud’s “Europe-west2-b” region, which knocked services offline early on Tuesday morning and caused intermittent network failures.

“A power event caused an outage within europe-west2-b zone. The power event is mitigated,” Google said. It later updated customers, saying the issue with impacted products had been reduced for most of those affected. “It is believed to be affecting currently a very small number of customers and our engineering team is working on it.”

Revolut was not the only company affected. In the UK, Lloyds Bank and HSBC users were also reporting issues to Downdetector, as well as DPD and the courts video platform used throughout the country.

AIB and Bank of Ireland said they were unaffected, and that all services were operating normally.

Google’s cloud division is competing with rivals Microsoft and AWS in providing cloud services to critical industries. This outage has brought the reliance of companies on a small number of cloud services back into the spotlight.

In October last year, a problem with AWS took down major apps such as Fortnite and Snapchat, along with banks, transport and messaging services. That was followed a week later by an issue at Microsoft Azure after an “inadvertent configuration change” caused problems for users.

]]>Bloomberg<![CDATA[Paddy Power owner Flutter to cut 240 jobs at Irish head office]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/paddy-power-owner-flutter-to-axe-1400-jobs-in-dublin-and-leeds/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/paddy-power-owner-flutter-to-axe-1400-jobs-in-dublin-and-leeds/Tue, 20 Oct 2026 12:18:58 +0000Paddy Power owner Flutter will cut 240 jobs from its Irish head office as it grapples with rising British betting taxes.

The group said on Tuesday that it planned to cut about 1,400 jobs in its UK and Ireland division to counter the impact of British government tax rises set to cost it $540 million (€480 million).

About 240 of those jobs will be lost in its Dublin office, while the group will also reduce numbers in the United Kingdom and in various centres around Europe, according to sources familiar with the business.

Flutter did not comment on the numbers that will be lost in each location.

However, an industry source estimated that up to 550 jobs could go in the UK, with the remaining cuts in Porto, Portugal, and Cluj-Napoca, Romania, Malta and Gibraltar, which service the UK and Ireland division.

Along with Paddy Power, the unit includes Betfair and Sky Bet.

Gaming and betting duty hikes announced by Britain’s Labour government will cost Flutter’s UK and Ireland unit $540 million this year, the group has already confirmed.

]]>Bilanol<![CDATA[More market disruption ahead as streamers go after live sports]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/media/2026/10/20/more-market-disruption-ahead-as-streamers-go-after-live-sports/https://www.irishtimes.com/media/2026/10/20/more-market-disruption-ahead-as-streamers-go-after-live-sports/Tue, 20 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000People have been predicting for a while now that it was only a matter of time before the big streaming platforms got serious about disrupting the lucrative live sports market. Until fairly recently, they seemed more interested in one-off marquee events than in longer-term licences. That’s now changing.

Last week, Netflix announced it had bought the rights to all 104 matches of the 2030 World Cup in Spain, which co-hosts the tournament with Portugal and Morocco. The price wasn’t disclosed. RTVE, the Spanish public broadcaster, reportedly paid €55 million for this summer’s tournament. Netflix already holds the North American rights to the next two women’s World Cups, and it is among a group of streamers preparing to take on Fox for the US rights to the 2030 and 2034 men’s tournaments, a bundle Fifa hopes might fetch as much as $4 billion.

Netflix executives spent years explaining why they didn’t need sport. Their first live forays were deliberately eye-catching: a Mike Tyson comeback fight here, a couple of NFL games on Christmas Day there. Then came a 10-year $5 billion deal for WWE wrestling, a slice of Major League Baseball and now the biggest football tournament on the planet in one of its main markets (Spain holds both the men’s and women’s World Cup titles).

Why the change of heart? Partly because Netflix and its rivals have run out of easy growth in mature markets. Keeping existing subscribers is just as important as finding new ones, and sport is the most reliable antidote for churn. People who binge a drama often cancel when it ends, but people who follow a team tend to stay for the whole season.

Then there’s advertising. Every big streamer now offers a cheaper tier carrying ads, and advertisers will pay a premium for audiences watching live in large numbers simultaneously. Sport is almost the only programming that delivers that any more. The irony is that the streamers did more than anyone to break the habit of collective, scheduled viewing. Now they are spending heavily to buy it back.

Watching the Premier League in Ireland is a strikingly costly business

The economics of sports rights explains why the price keeps rising inexorably. A league or federation sells something that cannot be replicated by a new entrant (no matter how hard the Saudis try). Rights are carved up by territory, by package and by platform to maximise the number of bidders. Those bidders need the property so badly that they overpay for it. The pay-TV model that Sky built around the Premier League in the 1990s established the principle of sport as the anchor holding an expensive bundle together.

Now the bundle is fraying. According to Ampere Analysis, streaming services will spend about $14.2 billion on sports rights this year. Amazon has overtaken DAZN as the biggest spender, and general entertainment platforms like Amazon, Netflix, Disney+, Apple and Paramount+ now account for 44 per cent of the total, up from 31 per cent last year. Their advantage over a specialist like DAZN, which has lost billions acquiring and distributing rights across Europe and Japan, is that sport doesn’t have to pay for itself. It only has to make the wider subscription more sticky. And a global platform can spread the cost across hundreds of millions of customers.

But the Spanish deal also shows the limits of exclusivity. Netflix will make one match each day free to watch, and will sub-licence a package to a free-to-air channel that includes every Spain game, both semi-finals and the final. This year’s final in New Jersey drew an average Spanish audience of more than 15 million. No sponsor wants to give up an audience on that scale, and neither does Fifa.

Nor does the law permit it. Under the EU’s audiovisual media rules, member states can draw up lists of events considered so important to society that they must be available on free television. Spain’s 2022 audiovisual law includes the World Cup semi-finals and final. So the Netflix deal recognises that obligation.

Ireland has its own version of these rules. Under section 162 of the Broadcasting Act 2009, designated events include the All-Ireland football and hurling finals, Ireland’s games at the World Cup and European Championship along with the opening games, semi-finals and finals of both tournaments. To qualify, a broadcaster must offer a free service reaching more than 90 per cent of the population. These lists were designed to stop Rupert Murdoch putting national shared moments behind a paywall. Whether they are fit for an era when the bidder is a global streamer, possibly one with a free tier of its own, is a question that can’t be avoided forever.

Irish soccer fans are already feeling the effects of fragmentation. From next year, anyone who wants to follow every Champions League game will need RTÉ, Premier Sports, Sky, Amazon Prime Video and Paramount+, which has taken the bulk of the British rights from TNT Sports. RTÉ has held on to its Wednesday night first pick, but it is now one tenant among many. In Gaelic games, GAAGO has shown how quickly matches viewers once took for granted can migrate behind a paywall and how vociferously the public objects when they do. All of this, of course, is welcome news for dodgy box vendors.

Make it easier to watch live sport in one place and you’ll do away with dodgy boxes

Free-to-air sport in Ireland is not going away. The designated list remains a protection, and RTÉ still has the reach that rights holders and sponsors value. But the new bidding war is changing the calculus. The streamers are bigger, richer and more strategically focused than the satellite companies ever were, and they’re no longer content to view live sport as an optional extra.

]]>Wu Hao<![CDATA[Social-housing pilot guarantees rent for landlords – but will they sign up?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/20/guaranteed-rent-on-offer-for-landlords-but-will-they-sign-up/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/20/guaranteed-rent-on-offer-for-landlords-but-will-they-sign-up/Tue, 20 Oct 2026 04:00:00 +0000A new pilot scheme, aimed at boosting the supply of social housing by offering a “secure, low-risk letting option” for landlords, has been launched by the Department of Housing.

Run by councils across Dublin for now, if it’s a success, it might be rolled out across the State.

Announcing the Dublin Rental Accommodation Scheme pilot scheme earlier this year, Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage James Browne said: “By encouraging more landlords to make their properties available, the pilot will help increase the supply of homes for individuals and families in need of social housing”.

But how does it work? Is it attractive for landlords? And with the rental market so tight, is it going to be enough to get landlords to commit to social housing?

Run on a pilot basis across the four Dublin local authority areas, the new rental accommodation scheme is being pitched as a “flexible, secure and financially attractive way to let residential properties”.

The tenant target is households that have received rent supplement for 18 months or more, and that have an ongoing housing need. The tenant pays an income-based differential rent contribution to the local authority, and the local authority pays the landlord the agreed rent.

The hope is that if more private landlords sign up for the scheme, more properties should become available to social housing tenants.

What’s different?

This is not the first time councils have looked to incentivise landlords to let their properties through local authorities. The rental accommodation scheme has two components – one working through approved housing boards letting their properties to councils and the other a private-sector arrangement whereby private landlords enter into rental agreements with local authorities.

It is the latter that the new pilot scheme is focusing on.

There have been challenges in attracting and retaining enough properties through the previous scheme. According to a review from the Department of Housing back in 2025, there has been a significant decline in the number of private landlords participating in it.

In 2023, for example, 1,004 landlords left the scheme but just 103 entered, leaving 7,010 tenancies. This compares to 11,231 back in 2018.

Three reasons for this are cited in the report: landlords selling the unit; tenants allocated social housing; and the landlord didn’t renew the contract.

And there are fewer landlords signing up, for reasons including rents on offer that are below market levels.

A spokeswoman for the Irish Property Owners Association (IPOA) says the scheme was “disadvantaged from the start” due to the rules set out in rent pressure zones. The maximum landlords could set rents at through the rental accommodation scheme was 92 per cent of market rent but this made it difficult to get back to a market rate, as only specified increases were allowed.

“It ended up that landlords were actually stuck with that sub-market rate due to rent pressure zones, which made the rent accommodation scheme unappealing,” she says.

HAP (housing assistance payment), on the other hand, had no such limits on the level rent was set at, as councils contribute a fixed amount and the tenant tops up the gap. This made it more attractive to landlords.

As a result, the new rent accommodation scheme pilot has been launched with some key differences. Firstly, landlords can charge local authorities up to 100 per cent of market rent. This rent is guaranteed, and will be paid “in full and on time” by the local authority – not the tenant.

And, if a tenant decides to leave, the council will pay the rent until a new tenant is placed.

Moreover, tenants will be sourced by the local authority, which means landlords won’t have to take on the task of vetting possible tenants.

The maximum length of a contract has also been extended, from four-to-six years previously to eight under the pilot scheme.

Rental payments will be front-loaded, so landlords won’t have to wait for their first payment. There will be better damage and compensation arrangements. And applications for the scheme will be more streamlined. Landlords will be responsible for managing the tenancy, and the property.

Is it enough?

County councils certainly hope it is. Pamela Kearns, mayor of South Dublin County Council, says the scheme will transform lives.

“Every property made available provides a vulnerable family, individual or senior with a safe, stable home in our community. While Dublin desperately needs housing, it also thrives on collaboration. Landlords now have a meaningful way to tackle housing shortages and build stronger communities. It is a true win for owners, tenants and Dublin as a whole.”

Already there has been “significant” interest in the new pilot, says the Department of Housing, with about 200 applications received by the end of September.

However, while the new scheme may have some key differences, groups representing property owners say it may not be enough to encourage landlords out of the private market and into guaranteed rent through the rental accommodation scheme.

“It looks very well on paper, but once you scratch the surface it’s not really like that,” says the spokeswoman for the IPOA, adding that there are a “couple of hurdles” that are making it unpalatable for landlords.

Firstly, the promise of full market rent is a “marketing strategy”, says the spokeswoman, because under the current legislation, a landlord can only charge market rent if they’re eligible for it, such as at the end of a six-year tenancy cycle. And if you’re not eligible then the council cannot override Residential Tenancies Board (RTB) rules.

Another issue is the length of the contract. A contract of a maximum eight years could mean that smaller landlords (ie those with four or fewer properties) could end up with a tenant for 12 years – even if the council drops out after eight. And larger landlords could have the tenant for life even if the council is no longer involved.

And if the tenancy wasn’t working out, such as if the tenant stopped paying rent, the IPOA spokeswoman says the landlord would need to go down the standard legal route, and issue a notice of termination. But it can take up to two years to get vacant possession of the property, she says.

However, the spokesman for the Department of Housing says tenancies can match up and “a six-year rent accommodation scheme agreement can align with the statutory cycle for small landlords with one to three tenancies, provided the relevant start dates coincide”.

For larger tenants, however, these new tenancies can only be ended for breaches of tenant obligations or because the property no longer meets the needs of the household’s accommodation needs.

Another challenge that might arise is that although the landlord doesn’t select their tenant, if things go wrong, they still have to sort it out. “The main landlord-tenant relationship ultimately remains the same between the property owner and the rental accommodation scheme tenant as it would with a typical private rented tenancy,” the scheme’s documentation states.

Forward payment is just two months, while other benefits can’t really be described as such, the IPOA argues. The offer of “100 per cent mortgage interest tax relief” is something all landlords are entitled to – while property tax is not eligible for a tax deduction.

Another factor, says the spokeswoman, is that the rental accommodation scheme has “very, very strict property standards enforcement”.

If an issue is identified – and according to the spokeswoman it could be something as relatively minor as the width set on window restrictors – rent payments will be suspended until the landlord gets its sorted.

The scheme is being run on a pilot basis until 2029 to see whether or not this additional flexibility will result in an increased flow of properties.

“This pilot allows us to test whether additional flexibility and stronger supports can increase property owner participation and expand the supply of homes available to social housing tenants,” the Minister said, adding that the results of the scheme would guide future national policy.

]]><![CDATA[Did the budget help a widow with two young children?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/20/did-the-budget-help-a-widow-with-two-young-children/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/20/did-the-budget-help-a-widow-with-two-young-children/Tue, 20 Oct 2026 04:00:00 +0000I am a widow with two young children, in my second year of widowhood. GM

Raising children is tough enough. Raising them on your own after having had to care for your husband when he was ill is a daunting challenge.

It’s at times like this that you hope a budget will deal a decisive blow in your favour, but, unfortunately for you and others who are financially vulnerable, this Government has sought to spread its largesse thinly and widely – hardly helped by the hospitality VAT cut last year limiting its room for manoeuvre this time around.

To make matters worse, although an exceptional tax credit is granted to new widows with children to try to ease the blow of two earners becoming one or the loss of joint assessment, the credit is phased down every year. And it does not appear to have been adjusted in the budget.

I should say this pension has now been renamed the bereaved partner’s (contributory) pension. It’s not just because someone in social protection decided the word “widow” needed changing: the pension is, since last year, now available also to cohabiting couples where one partner has died.

If they don’t have children, they must have been together for five years, or, for those with dependent children, two years.

Widows under the age of 66 get between €252.60 and €259.50 weekly, depending on the number of PRSI stamps they have. Those over the age of 66 get a payment of between €286.60 and €299.30.

If, like you, they have dependent children, they get €58 a week for each child under the age of 12 and €78 for older children.

Anyway, along with most other welfare payments, this payment will rise by €10 from January of next year. So, if you are on the maximum payment for someone under 66, it will rise to €269.50 a week. As a result, you will get an additional €22 a week, or just shy of €1,150 a year, unless one of your children turns 12 next year. It’s not nothing, but if, as you say, you are paying tax on this money, it doesn’t really stretch too far.

If your children are in childcare or after-school care with a creche that is signed up to the Government’s core funding model, that cost will come down next year but not until September.

On top of that, you will also benefit from the employee or earned income tax credit, which is rising by €125 a year to €2,125.

Is my €1,000 monthly childcare bill really falling to €550?

There is also a benefit from the widening of the standard rate income tax band. As a widow, you pay 20 per cent income tax up to €48,000, which is better than the €44,000 for a single person, but short of the €53,000 you would have had as a married couple with one person working.

From January, your 20 per cent band will increase to €50,500, which will cut your tax bill by €500 as long as you are earning above that €50,500 level.

On the flip side, PRSI is rising for all employees although there will be a modest cut in your Universal Social Charge.

All told, you will be around €950 better off next year, leaving aside childcare, which may or may not be relevant.

I say “we”, even though I am a transplanted Australian, one of the more than 40 per cent of Londoners who are foreign-born. London Southend Airport, which I have never technically been to, means we have six airports. There are also more than 80 Michelin-starred restaurants and, by Cvent’s count, 200 museums, 270 theatres, 857 art galleries and four Unesco World Heritage sites. In 1994, he set up a memorial fund (hosting a golf event recently in Druids Glen) in the names of his parents that has raised more than $5 million for good causes, and has been a big supporter of the Ireland Funds (of which he is a former chairman) over many decades, supporting projects on both sides of the Border.

Many who know Fitzpatrick consider him to be a workaholic. “People say that but I don’t know. Maybe I am. I’ve sacrificed certain things in my life to keep things going. But at the end of the day, I’m happy and I love what I do,” he says.

Now 65, is he considering retirement?

“Some people are happy to retire. Don’t get me wrong, I’d like to slow down, no doubt. Over the last few years I’ve got a really good team around me. I delegate a bit better now. I’m still on the phone every day but I trust the team around me.

“Do I want to work until I’m 80? Absolutely not. Do I want to slow down? Yes. But I do have to get out some time.

“My father worked until he was 72, which wasn’t late, and then died at 75. You think, ‘What’s the point of all this?’ I want to enjoy life as well but I enjoy what I do. I’m not going to work until the end of my time but at the moment I’m happy.”

He namechecks some of the senior Irish staff who have worked with him for years: group general manager Shane Cookman; Chris O’Sullivan, GM of the Manhattan property; Patrick Leyden, GM at the Grand Central; and his finance chief Peter Kidd.

“As long as I have a strong team with me I’m happy. The two hotels are running perfectly, they are within 10 blocks of each other and I can walk between them.

“I have two beautiful properties in midtown Manhattan, and they’re building all around me. Eventually, someone might come in and make me an offer, maybe not for a hotel but for something else. But I’m not in any hurry. I’ve a another good eight to 10 years. I can guarantee that I’m not going to get into my 80s and still be at it.”

Getting a majority will be difficult between those member states who want a bigger, and others a smaller, budget. There is, however, an urgency to strike a deal before possible changes in government after forthcoming elections make reaching agreement even more challenging.

Marine le Pen, for example, believes in dramatically reducing the EU’s role and returning powers to national governments. If she wins the French presidential election next May, she could seek to upend EU funding.

To judge by the rows over recent decades about the EU’s budget, you might believe it is a major drain on member states’ national resources. However, the budget amounts to only 1.1 per cent of national income, whereas national budgets across the EU average 45 per cent of national income, somewhat higher than for Ireland.

So the fight over whether the budget should amount to 1 per cent or 1.25 per cent of national income is about relatively small sums when averaged across the EU. In national budgets, such a small difference as a share of national income could get lost in rounding errors.

There are a range of public goods that are best undertaken on a pan-EU basis rather than by national governments. Examples include cross-border infrastructure, research and development, climate, security, foreign policy, industrial policy and development aid. These are areas where collective EU spending is more effective than uncoordinated national investment.

European Commission unhappy with EU budget but Taoiseach says compromise had to be made

The construction of the electricity interconnector between Ireland and France is a prime example that merits the significant EU funding involved. This project will benefit not only Ireland and France, but also the wider EU electricity system.

Interconnection across borders boosts efficiency, provides better matching of variable supply and demand, and minimises wasted power generation.

Other potentially beneficial projects to enable the free flow of electricity across the EU’s national boundaries are only likely to proceed if there is EU financial support.

Food shortages in the aftermath of the second World War were the initial driving force behind the EU’s Common Agricultural Policy. Today, however, it is more difficult to justify rationally why agriculture looms so large in the EU’s budget, or why the EU rather than national governments should fund farm supports.

Europe rearms: files reveal extent of plans for a new ‘defence union’

Ireland, of course, has benefited disproportionately from EU payments to farmers over the past half century. Like other EU members, we pay about 1 per cent of national income into the EU budget. However, despite the fact that we are one of the richest EU members, we get back around 0.7 per cent of national income, most of it going to Irish farmers. A great deal.

The modernising of Ireland’s infrastructure has also benefited greatly from EU support to poorer regions over the first decades of EU membership.

Today there are two groups of countries with very different outlooks on the EU’s budget.

The “frugals”, like Scandinavia, Germany and the Netherlands, want a smaller budget, in particular they want to cut back on funds for agriculture, and for infrastructure in poorer states. They want to reallocate funds to other headings.

The “friends of cohesion”, which include Spain, Italy and some poorer member states, want a larger budget, with continuing substantial agriculture and cohesion payments.

The first stab at a compromise by the Irish presidency involved a small cut in the original EU Commission budget proposal. For 2028-34, this proposed that real EU resources, after debt interest, would be slightly lower than today.

The Irish Times view on the EU budget: a key task for Ireland’s presidency

This draft also largely protected agriculture and cohesion funds. But this compromise got a widespread thumbs down.

In the next round of negotiations, Ireland needs to adjust its proposals to garner more support. Next time, the Bruegel think tank in Brussels suggests, we should propose a slightly larger budget that cuts back on agriculture and cohesion funds, which are unpopular with the frugals, and that reallocates some resources to other European public goods.

A few rounds of proposals may be needed to garner the necessary majority support before year end.

As the honest broker, it may thus fall to the Irish Government to propose a compromise budget that would cut some resources for agriculture, which will be unpopular at home.

However, given the risk that delayed agreement could mean an even more unpalatable outcome, as the political winds shift in France and elsewhere, it is vital from an Irish point of view that agreement is reached on the budget by the end of the year. Better a budget with somewhat reduced funds for agriculture, than no budget and no funds.

]]>LockieCurrie<![CDATA[AI fever is producing some strange symptoms]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/19/ai-fever-is-producing-some-strange-symptoms/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/19/ai-fever-is-producing-some-strange-symptoms/Mon, 19 Oct 2026 04:00:00 +0000“A lot of investors have no clue what they are investing in,” Broadcom chief executive Hock Tan warned this week, saying they set “very extreme expectations” only to discover that the AI trade resembles a casino.

The comments were unusually forthright, although a few critical remarks would not normally be enough to send shares in mega-cap technology giants such as Samsung (down 7.4 per cent on the day) and SK Hynix (down 10.1 per cent) tumbling.

In truth, there was more to the declines than Tan’s comments, with concerns about Chinese competition, the sustainability of AI spending and Samsung’s latest earnings report all weighing on the sector, but the swings certainly highlighted the fragility of AI-related sentiment.

Meanwhile, Tan’s reference to “very extreme expectations” may have been aimed at investors, but extraordinary expectations of AI are apparently evident elsewhere in the industry. Shyam Sankar, chief technology officer of data analytics giant Palantir, claims some AI researchers have taken up smoking to signal their conviction that artificial intelligence would eventually cure cancer – an example, he said, of the “mass psychosis” and “social delusion” around AI.

Then there is Anthropic, which is moving to prohibit sustained cruelty towards its Claude chatbot, despite the absence of evidence that the software experiences suffering.

Clueless investors with extreme expectations are one thing, but researchers smoking in anticipation of a cure for cancer and developers worrying about a chatbot’s feelings suggest the AI boom is acquiring some distinctly unusual characteristics.

   <title>„True Crime“ als Türöffner in die Antike</title>
   <description>In der großen Herbstausstellung „Tatort Ephesos" holt das Kunsthistorische Museum (KHM) seine Antikensammlung und die Ägyptisch-Orientalische Sammlung erstmals gemeinsam vor den Vorhang. Das Ergebnis ist nicht ganz so „True Crime", wie der Ankündigungstext verspricht. Leading figures from Poland’s ruling coalition have hit back at US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth over his recent remarks downplaying the contribution of America’s allies during the war in Afghanistan.

The speaker of parliament, Włodzimierz Czarzasty, called the comments “scandalous”, while Prime Minister Donald Tusk read out a message sent to him by a Polish army medic who was serving in Afghanistan when the last of 44 Polish soldiers who died there was declared dead.

💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️

Chciałbym, żeby te słowa dotarły do naszych sojuszników, żeby już nigdy więcej nikt nie lekceważył wysiłku naszych żołnierzy. pic.twitter.com/gGJkh4Gnft

— Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 20, 2026

The controversy stemmed from a speech the US defence secretary gave to US military cadets in Tennessee on Saturday. Hegseth referred to his time serving as a US Army officer in Afghanistan, where he recalled that the International Security Assistance Force (ISAF) headquarters had flags from over fifty countries.

“Except,” Hegseth said, “there were maybe five [countries] that contributed. It was actually closer to one or two that actually, by the end, were involved in kinetic operations. In fact, the patch ‘ISAF’ – we joked that it meant ‘I Saw Americans Fighting.'”

The comments earned quick reproach from Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski, who aimed a message at Hegseth on social media, saying: “Tell that to the families of 44 Polish soldiers who died securing the tough Ghazni province.”

Tell that, Mr @SecWar, to the families of 44 Polish soldiers who died securing the tough Ghazni province. https://t.co/vm4TM0sMJO

— Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) October 18, 2026

On Tuesday, the remarks earned even stronger reproach from Czarzasty, who is the speaker of the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, and the leader of The Left (Lewica), one of the groups that forms Poland’s ruling coalition.

At a press conference, Czarzasty said that Hegseth’s “scandalous” comments are “harmful to the families of Polish soldiers and to Polish national pride”.

He also criticised President Karol Nawrocki – an opponent of the government and conservative ally of Donald Trump – for not condemning Hegseth’s remarks.

It is “an insult to Polish soldiers” that Nawrocki, who serves as commander-in-chief, “is unable to stand up for their dignity and the dignity of those who died”, declared Czarzasty.

To skandaliczne, że prezydent Polski boi się potępić polityków amerykańskich za brak szacunku do polskich żołnierzy, którzy zginęli w Afganistanie. pic.twitter.com/uyv54yDvrI

— Włodzimierz Czarzasty 📚📖 (@wlodekczarzasty) October 20, 2026

Later on Tuesday, Tusk read out to his cabinet a text message he said he had received from a former military medic, whom he did not name.

“Please stand up for soldiers, I beg you,” wrote the medic. “During my tour in Afghanistan, we confirmed the death of the last Polish casualty, a platoon sergeant whose wife was pregnant in Poland at the time.”

“I received a medal from the Americans for helping them, for treating Americans. I didn’t have to do that. We treated them with our own Polish medicines,” they added.

Tusk then added his own remarks, stating: “I would like these words to reach our allies. So that no one will ever again downplay the efforts of our soldiers. Wherever our allies, including our closest ally, the Americans, have needed our participation, Polish soldiers stood shoulder to shoulder with them.”

Tusk also referenced Nawrocki’s silence on the matter. “Frankly, I was also counting on the president speaking out on this matter. But it seems I miscalculated.”

 

Tusk is the first European head of government to directly criticise Hegseth’s remarks, although a spokesperson for British Prime Minister Andy Burnham did say on Monday that it was “wrong to diminish the role” of British personnel, 457 of whom died in Afghanistan.

Of the 3,621 coalition deaths during the war in Afghanistan, around two thirds were Americans (2,461). The rest came from 31 different countries, with Poland’s 44 fatalities the seventh most of any nation.

Hegseth’s remarks are not the first time that the Trump administration has caused anger in Poland by downplaying allies’ role in Afghanistan. In January, Trump himself suggested that other countries had “stayed a little back, a little off the front lines”.

That prompted General Roman Polko, who commanded Poland’s GROM special forces unit in Iraq and Afghanistan, to call the US president “a coward who has never been on the front lines”.

The former commander of Poland's special forces in Iraq and Afghanistan has condemned Donald Trump for questioning the contribution of America's allies

"This is the cynicism of a coward who hasn’t been on the front lines himself," said General @PolkoRoman https://t.co/kElkAO5qX4

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 23, 2026

The Polish government has also clashed with the US on other issues. In January, Tusk joined other European leaders in calling for Greenland’s sovereignty to be respected, following Trump’s calls for the island to be brought under US control.

The following month, Tusk declared that Poland would not be a “vassal” of the US and suggested that Nawrocki wanted Poland to be too subservient to Washington. Czarzasty has twice this year clashed with the US ambassador over critical remarks he made towards Trump.

However, at the same time, the Polish government has sought to maintain positive relations with Washington, given America’s role as Poland’s most important security partner. In June, Poland formally requested that the US establish a new permanent military base on its territory.

Hegseth himself has praised Poland, calling it a “model ally” last year. The US State Department this month also announced that it was pushing for Poland to be allowed to join the G20 “as soon as possible”, pointing to its “growing leadership position in the international arena”.

A member of Poland’s military reserve force has been detained for alleged espionage.

On Monday afternoon, following media reports of the arrest, a spokesman for the military police confirmed that they had detained a 31-year-old man of Polish and Ukrainian citizenship, who holds the rank of senior private reserve.

The suspect, who had at the time been undertaking a course at the Military Medical Academy (WAM) in Łódź, is being held on suspicion of declaring readiness to act for the benefit of a foreign intelligence service against Poland. That crime is punishable by up to eight years in prison.

W dniu 16 października 2026 r. żołnierze z Oddziału Żandarmerii Wojskowej w Łodzi, zgodnie z postanowieniem Prokuratora Działu do Spraw Wojskowych Prokuratury Rejonowej Łódź-Polesie w Łodzi, dokonali zatrzymania mężczyzny w wieku 31 lat, obywatelstwa polskiego i ukraińskiego, w… pic.twitter.com/MLpqzfT4iO

By Daniel Tilles

Poland will hold parliamentary elections a year from now. The outcome will decide who governs the country for the next four years – although, given how close the polls are, and with questions over coalition formation, it could also result in uncertainty, chaos, and even new elections being called.

Below, we explain how the elections work, which parties will be standing, what kind of outcomes are possible, and which issues may animate the campaign.

When will the election take place?

Assuming early elections are not called, the vote must take place on a non-working day in the last 30 days before the end of the current four-year parliamentary term, which began on 13 November 2023.

Because elections in Poland are held on Sundays, that gives four possible dates: 17, 24 or 31 October, or 7 November (though 1 November and 11 November, which are public holidays, are also theoretically possible).

It is the president, Karol Nawrocki, who will choose the date. He must do so no later than 90 days before the end of the current parliamentary term.

How does voting work?

The 460 members of the more powerful lower house, the Sejm, are elected through proportional representation, meaning that seats are distributed more or less on the basis of the share of the vote parties receive (using the so-called D’Hondt method for allocating seats from electoral lists put forward by each party). However, parties must receive at least 5% of the vote nationally to enter parliament (a figure that rises to 8% for coalitions of parties who stand on a single electoral list).

The 100 members of the upper-house Senate are chosen through a first-past-the-post system similar to how members of the US Congress or British House of Commons are elected, with the candidate in each district that receives the most votes winning the seat.

How is a government formed?

A government can only be formed if it can win a vote of confidence in the Sejm.

After the elections, the president designates a prime minister, who is tasked with forming a government – which would almost certainly be made up of a coalition of parties – that must then win a vote of confidence.

If they fail to do so (as happened in 2023), the Sejm votes to choose an alternative prime minister, who likewise must try to form a government that has the confidence of the Sejm.

Parliament has chosen @donaldtusk as Poland's new prime minister.

That paves the way for him to form a new government in the coming days, ending the eight-year rule of the national-conservative PiS party https://t.co/iZUKh2rxnP

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 11, 2023

If that fails, the president has a second chance to pick a prime minister, who must again win a confidence vote. However, whereas the previous two votes require an absolute majority (większość bezwzględna) to be carried, this time only a simple majority is needed, making it easier to form a minority government.

If this third and final attempt does not work, then parliament is dissolved and new elections are called.

Who is likely to form the next government?

At the moment, it is incredibly difficult to say. Polls suggest an even split in support between parties generally aligned with Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition – which ranges from left to centre right – and the right-wing opposition. However, the 5% electoral threshold complicates the picture.

According to current polling averages compiled by Polish website eWybory and Politico Europe, Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) leads with 32%. One of its coalition partners, The Left (Lewica), is on 7%, while two others, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL) and centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), are on around 3% and 1%, respectively. Another left-wing party, Together (Razem), which previously caucused with the ruling coalition but split in 2024, is on around 4%.

Meanwhile, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, is on 20%. Two far-right opposition groups, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), have 14% and 9%, respectively. The right-wing Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), which broke away from PiS this year, is at around 5%.

Rolling 30-day average support in polls for Poland’s main political parties (source: eWybory.eu)

If we treat those as two potential blocs, parties more or less aligned with the current government are on around 47% while the right-wing opposition is on 48%. However, PSL and Poland 2050 currently look likely to fall below the 5% threshold if they stand alone, meaning votes for them would not count. That would significantly harm Tusk’s chances of forming a new government. If Rozwój Plus stood alone and fell below the threshold, that would harm the opposition.

It is therefore likely that, as the elections draw nearer, parties that seem likely to fall below 5% will seek to join forces with other groups. In 2023, PSL and Poland 2050 stood together in the so-called Third Way (Trzecia Droga) alliance. But they have made clear they do not intend to do that again. That leaves them with limited options. They could join forces with KO on a single electoral list, but that does not guarantee that their voters will follow them. Indeed, some may baulk at voting for Tusk’s party.

The Polish People's Party's parliamentary survival is on a knife edge, and could determine whether @donaldtusk's coalition remains in power after next year's elections.@AleksSzczerbiak looks at the challenges facing PSL and how it may respond to them https://t.co/MmswSLNWJE

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 30, 2026

Meanwhile, there are some wildcards in the pack. KKP, led by radical-right extremist Grzegorz Braun, is shunned by the mainstream right for its antisemitism, anti-Americanism and sympathy towards Russia. PiS’s leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, has declared that he would not allow Braun to join government. Development Plus has taken a similar position. Both parties value relations with the US and the Trump administration, whose ambassador to Poland has reportedly pushed them to rule out working with Braun.

However, if KKP maintains its current level of support, it looks almost impossible for the opposition to form a parliamentary majority without it, meaning there would be a strong temptation to somehow work with Braun. Kaczyński’s determination to remove Tusk from power may outweigh his dislike of Braun and desire to keep the Americans onside.

The Together party – if it manages to pass the 5% threshold – could likewise represent a challenge for Tusk when forming a coalition, given that it has criticised the government for failing to keep promises on healthcare spending, public sector pay, and liberalising the abortion law.

 

There also remains the possibility of some elements from each camp joining the other side – either entire parties or individual MPs defecting – in order to help form a government.

PiS has long sought to tempt PSL to its side (and recent reports suggest that even President Donald Trump tried to persuade PSL’s leader, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, to do so). It is conceivable that Rozwój Plus could work with parts of the current ruling camp, though its hatred of Tusk would make that very difficult.

All of the difficulties outlined above mean there is a significant chance that it will not be possible for anyone to form a government, necessitating fresh elections – something that has never happened before in Poland. If that happens, it would mean uncertainty and a lack of clear leadership at a time when Poland is facing major security challenges and a worsening fiscal situation.

What about the Senate?

The Senate, like the Sejm, is currently controlled by the ruling coalition. Indeed, Tusk has an even larger majority there than in the lower house, making it harder for the opposition to flip. Although the Senate is much weaker than the Sejm – and control of it does not determine who forms the government – it does have some powers that make it a useful asset.

It can slow down the passage of legislation, though not block it. The Senate also must approve the appointment of certain officials, such as the heads of the Supreme Audit Office (NIK) and the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), as well as the Commissioner for Human Rights (RPO).

In a rare clash between Poland’s two houses of parliament, in both of which the government has a majority, the Senate has rejected a candidate chosen by the Sejm to become the new head of the state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) https://t.co/QUsqfDNh4s

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 7, 2026

The upper house is also required to approve proposals by the president to hold national referendums. This year, the Senate has twice blocked moves by Nawrocki to hold a referendum on EU climate policies.

In a situation where Tusk’s coalition controlled the Sejm, and was therefore still in government, but the right-wing opposition held the Senate, that would give the president a powerful tool to call referendums on policies important to him and the opposition.

To that end, there have been calls for the right-wing and far-right opposition to form a so-called Senate pact, of the type that Tusk and his allies used to win control of the upper house in 2019 and 2023.

What that means in practice is that the parties forming the pact agree to stand only one candidate between them in each of the 100 Senate districts, making it more likely that they will scoop up votes from supporters of all the parties in the pact and win the winner-takes-all contest.

What role will Nawrocki play in all of this?

Presidents are in theory expected to be non-partisan. In practice, however, they will seek to boost parties or coalitions aligned with them, and with whom it will be easier to work.

Since Nawrocki was elected last year, relations and cooperation between the president and government have reached unprecedently low levels. Within just 10 months, Nawrocki had vetoed more bills than any previous president in history over their entire terms. He has made it abundantly clear that he would prefer to work with a government formed from the right-wing opposition.

During his first year, President Nawrocki has transformed his office into a centre of resistance to the government and become a unifying figure for the fragmented right.

But he faces new challenges moving towards the next election, writes @AleksSzczerbiak https://t.co/uNYrFOppSp

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 7, 2026

However, the extent to which he will be involved in the election campaign is unclear. Some figures on the right hope that Nawrocki will act as a figurehead, using his positive relations with parties across the right-wing opposition to bring them together.

In practical terms, this could involve him acting as the patron of a Senate pact (something the head of Nawrocki’s cabinet recently said the president was willing to do), as well as helping right-wing parties form a coalition government after the elections.

Nawrocki also continues to enjoy strong approval ratings among the conservative electorate, meaning that his presence during the election campaign could act as a boost for the opposition.

What issues are likely to feature in the campaign?

A major issue will be the question of sovereignty. The right-wing opposition accuses Tusk of being Brussels’ and Berlin’s lapdog, handing over ever more power to the EU and prioritising Germany’s interests over Poland’s.

The ruling coalition, meanwhile, argues that PiS is too beholden to the Trump administration and warns that the opposition is pushing Poland towards “Polexit” from the EU, which would leave the country isolated and vulnerable, as well as much poorer.

Those battle lines extend to security policy too, with the Tusk government shifting emphasis towards Europe as a defence partner but PiS insisting that only the US can truly guarantee Poland’s security. Poland’s desire to host a new permanent US military base has already become highly politicised. If progress stalls, the opposition will blame the government. If Washington confirms that the base will go ahead, Nawrocki will seek to take the credit, based on his good relationship with Trump.

On this point, though, it is worth noting the split within the opposition. While PiS and Rozwój Plus are strongly pro-American, Confederation and, to an even greater extent, KKP, are opposed to a greater US presence in Poland.

President @NawrockiKn says that a planned new permanent US military base in Poland is “confirmed” because his American counterpart, Donald Trump, is “famous for keeping his word”.

He also suggested that the new facility will be called “Fort Trump” https://t.co/uGGJSBe5nr

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 23, 2026

Where the right-wing opposition has been united, however, is on pushing for a tougher position towards Ukraine and Ukrainian refugees in Poland.

While tensions have calmed significantly since the crisis sparked in May by President Volodymyr Zelensky naming a military unit after a group that massacred Poles in World War Two, it is likely that relations with Ukraine and the large-scale presence of Ukrainians in Poland will remain important issues during the election campaign.

The ruling coalition, meanwhile, will be keen to emphasise its tough overall approach to immigration, which it says was out of control under the former PiS government. It can point to the falling number of new residence permits being issued, the growing number of deportations, and tougher measures on the Belarus border, including a ban on asylum claims.

Poland has forcibly removed 2,100 foreigners from the country this year, around twice as many as in 2024.

The figures come after the government introduced a tougher new migration policy last year, which has included more deportations of foreign criminals https://t.co/zOBxPLipy8

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 31, 2025

The economy, public finances and cost of living are also likely to be major issues.

As long as the current global energy crisis sparked by the conflict around Iran continues, the opposition will seek to place the blame for record fuel prices on the government. They will also cite large deficits and the ballooning public debt as evidence that Tusk is mismanaging the economy.

The ruling coalition will point to continued strong economic growth and blame Nawrocki, who has vetoed revenue-generating tax bills, for the fiscal situation.

City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Tue, 20 Oct 2026 21:56:53 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.0.7 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 Union fury at Natwest plans for staff to attend the office TWO DAYS a week https://www.cityam.com/natwest-facing-backlash-from-union-after-ordering-staff-into-office-twice-a-week/ Tue, 20 Oct 2026 17:44:42 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2467423

Natwest is facing backlash from trade union Unite over a new plan to require workers to attend the office for a mandatory two days a week. On Tuesday Unite, which represents over 1 million workers across private, public, and voluntary sectors, including some Natwest employees, said the lender’s decision was “out of touch with the [...]]]>

Natwest is facing backlash from trade union Unite over a new plan to require workers to attend the office for a mandatory two days a week.

On Tuesday Unite, which represents over 1 million workers across private, public, and voluntary sectors, including some Natwest employees, said the lender’s decision was “out of touch with the realities facing its workforce.”

From February next year, all employees at the bank will be required to work from the office for two days a week.

Some employees at the FTSE 100 bank who are ‘remote-first’ workers are currently required to attend the office for two days a month, which will no longer be the case when the new policy comes into force.

It is the latest example of firms calling workers back into the office after widespread work from home orders during the pandemic.

But Unite general secretary Sharon Graham said the move is “yet another kick in the teeth for workers who have suffered years of real-terms pay cuts and who are struggling to make ends meet.”

“Natwest’s decision is completely out of touch with the realities facing its workforce. Thousands of workers face higher travel and childcare costs and disruption to caring responsibilities,” Graham said.

Natwest ‘must ditch’ office attendance plans

Graham added Natwest “must ditch these proposals and engage properly with its workers.”

 “For Natwest to impose these changes while reneging on existing agreements shows complete contempt for its workforce,” Graham said.

Nearly 17,300 staff at the bank follow a hybrid working pattern where they are required to attend the office at least three days a fortnight, and a further 13,500 are remote-first, roles which are only required to attend the office twice a month.

The remainder of its UK staff, which includes those in customer facing roles, those working in branches, and other customer-facing roles including traders, must already go in to the office least four days a week.

“We recognise this will be a change for some colleagues and we’re giving them time to plan ahead and will support them through the transition,” a Natwest spokesman said.

“Flexible working remains an important part of how we work, but we’ve also learnt more about the value that spending time together brings for our colleagues and customers,” the spokesperson added.

]]> 2467423Rosie Harris-Davison Rosie Harris-Davison Nscale eyes second $45bn deal with Anthropic after Microsoft setback https://www.cityam.com/nscale-eyes-second-45bn-deal-with-anthropic-after-microsoft-setback/ Tue, 20 Oct 2026 15:55:37 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2467324

British AI infrastructure firm, Nscale, is in talks to secure a second $45bn (£33.5bn) computing deal with Anthropic, just a day after Microsoft pulled out of its flagship UK data centre project. The Nvidia-backed company is negotiating an agreement to supply the US AI giant with computing power from a second facility at its Monarch [...]]]>

British AI infrastructure firm, Nscale, is in talks to secure a second $45bn (£33.5bn) computing deal with Anthropic, just a day after Microsoft pulled out of its flagship UK data centre project.

The Nvidia-backed company is negotiating an agreement to supply the US AI giant with computing power from a second facility at its Monarch campus in West Virginia. The proposed deal would cover 460 megawatts of capacity powered by Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin chips, potentially doubling Anthropic’s Nscale commitments to almost $90bn.

The agreement could be signed within days, though discussions remain ongoing and terms could change, as reported by Bloomberg.

The talks follow an initial $44.6bn agreement signed in August, under which Anthropic agreed to lease computing capacity from the same West Virginia campus over six years.

The potential contract comes at a critical moment for London-founded Nscale, which is preparing for a blockbuster New York stock market listing amid growing scrutiny of the vast sums being spent on AI infrastructure.

The company reportedly targets a valuation of up to $30bn, although some investors have pushed for a lower figure between $16bn and $19bn.

Nscale and Anthropic have not commented on this deal.

Nscale faces mounting pressure ahead of IPO

The negotiations come just a day after Microsoft withdrew from plans to develop what was billed as Britain’s largest AI data centre in Loughton, Essex, dealing a blow to one of the UK’s flagship AI infrastructure projects.

The £2bn development, announced last year and championed by the government, has been delayed by issues with its electricity grid connection.

Nscale said it remained committed to the project despite Microsoft’s withdrawal.

“Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts”, a spokesperson said.

Microsoft also stressed that the decision related to a single site, adding that it remained committed to its wider partnership with Nscale.

The setback has raised questions about the company’s ability to deliver its ambitious data centre pipeline. Last week, Bloomberg reported that construction at Nscale’s flagship Norwegian facility in Glomfjord was six months behind schedule following technical problems, including cooling system leaks and a fire.

The company reported a $1bn net loss on $141m in revenue in the first half of 2026, while its IPO filings showed it had yet to secure financing for the infrastructure needed to fulfil its first Anthropic contract.

Under that agreement, Anthropic can terminate the deal if Nscale fails to meet certain financing and operational milestones.

The proposed second contract would therefore represent a significant vote of confidence in Nscale’s expansion plans, although the company would still need to secure funding for the additional computing infrastructure.

The talks also underscore the growing financial commitments underpinning the AI boom, as developers race to secure the computing power needed to train and run more advanced models.

Anthropic has struck several multibillion-dollar infrastructure agreements as demand for its Claude AI models grows, while investors have become increasingly concerned about the debt and execution risks facing data centre developers.

CHELTENHAM returns this week with the two-day Showcase Meeting signalling that the jumps season is getting into gear.

It looks like there could be plenty of rain around, and the going may change dramatically from the current description of good, so it’s worth keeping a close eye on the forecast.

There’s plenty of interest across both Friday and Saturday at Cheltenham, but at the moment the first day looks to present the best chance of an ante-post bet.

That opportunity comes in the squareintheair.com Handicap Chase (3.35pm), a race that the Dan Skelton-trained CALICO has won for the last two years.

Skelton is a brilliant target trainer and in both the last two renewals of this valuable prize, he has primed Calico to be at his best.

Last year, he was an impressive seven-length winner off a mark of 142, and he comes into this contest six pounds higher in the weights.

He won a big handicap off a higher mark than this at Ascot last season, though, so it might not be enough to derail his hat-trick bid.

The thing that stands out about this 10-year-old is he is best when fresh.

He has a record of 82211 on his seasonal return and this race will have been his long-term target.

The Skelton yard is flying along, having already passed the 100-winner mark for the season, and their horses look to hold a fitness edge over many of their rivals at this stage of the campaign.

There is clearly plenty in Calico’s favour, and while he is best on good ground, he was a winner last year on good-to-soft, so will hopefully be fine if the worst of the rain misses Prestbury Park.

The 4/1 on offer looks fair at this stage as I can see him going off nearly half that price on the day.

There’s also some competitive action on the flat at Doncaster on Friday.

In the opening six-furlong nursery (1.35pm), Bulletsnap and Captaincy look the pair to beat and they head the betting.

However, there could be something lurking at a bigger price here and MIND THOSE STEPS looks like an interesting prospect.

Tim Easterby’s colt has shown form on soft and heavy going, so it won’t be a worry if the rain gets into the ground on Town Moor.

His close-up third on handicap debut at Ayr last month was a good effort, as was his sixth-place finish in the Listed Redcar Two-Year-Old Trophy behind Satellite Of Love last time.

If running to a similar level, he looks a big price at 16/1, now that he drops in class, and he is worth supporting each-way.

INVICTUS GOLD is another worthy of a second look in the seven-furlong handicap (2.45pm).

Tom Clover’s four-year-old hasn’t got his head in front since May last year, but he definitely suffered at the hands of the handicapper after being put up 11 pounds for that impressive success.

Several of his runs this season have been good efforts, most notably an excellent second to the progressive Sondad at Epsom in June off a mark of 99.

Now three pounds lower in the weights, he looks to be dropping to a mark he can strike off, and conditions at Doncaster promise to suit.

He handles soft ground well so any rain that falls would be welcome, while this step up to seven furlongs for the first time might help eke out a bit more improvement.

At 16/1, he’s another each-way pick that should outrun his odds.

Calico                                                3.35pm               Cheltenham

DONCASTER on Saturday plays host to the final Group One contest of the flat season, the William Hill Futurity Trophy (1.30pm).

Unsurprisingly, Aidan O’Brien currently has an embarrassment of riches in the contest, with 11 of the 17 entries being Ballydoyle representatives.

Noble Exhibit is the current ante-post favourite, but with rain forecast towards the back of the week, the ground could go against the son of Frankel, who hasn’t encountered anything worse than yielding conditions.

One who would benefit from any rain is Karl Burke’s BURNING UP.

He created a good impression on his first two career starts, winning in commanding fashion, and then ran with credit in the Group Two Royal Lodge Stakes at Newmarket.

He was patently unsuited by the track that day, when rolling around as he encountered the dip, but got organised and rallied to finish second.

That would have taught him a lot and, returning to a flatter track, he looks good value at 5/1 in a contest that will cut up at the declaration stage.

LUNA A INBHIR NIS returns to shallower waters in the opening five-furlong handicap (12.55pm), having been tried in the Group One Prix de l’Abbaye on Arc weekend.

Trainer Katie Scott has had a brilliant year, and she has developed this horse into a classy sprinter.

She goes well in softer conditions and still looks to be well enough treated on a mark of 99.

Finishing 11th in Paris was a solid effort, considering she was just over four lengths behind the principals, and split Rumstar and Redorange, who have plied their trade in far deeper company than this.

She may well be able to take advantage of an unchanged mark, and at 9/1 is a cracking each-way bet.

Ahead of this year’s Toast the City Awards, celebrating the best of the Square Mile, we go inside Boulebar Spitalfields

As the experience economy accelerates, with axe throwing, darts and cricket themed bars launching, the latest brings the French game of pétanque to Spitalfields.

Boulebar Spitalfields offers Londoners new ways to drink and socialise while playing interactive games, the type popularised in the town squares of regional France.

The bar has 10 pétanque courts as well as authentic French food and Parisian themed cocktails in an underground space beneath the Victorian cobbles of Spitalfields.

Boulebar Spitalfields: the classic French game in London

The game of pétanque is easy to pick up: it involves throwing metal balls called boules in the direction of a small wooden ball called the cochonnet, or jack.

Its simplicity is what makes it attractive to diverse groups of locals in town squares, who bond over the game no matter their political views, jobs or upbringing.

Dishes on the menu include the ‘Tour De France’ cheese and charcuterie selection, moules marinieres, steak frite and steak hache. Cocktails include one described as a “Solero for adults”, a watermelon picante and a lillet rose spritz.

Food and drink packages are also available for bigger groups of corporates, friends and families.

Encouraging “friendly rivalry and laughter”, pétanque is the latest experience to be ‘gamified’ in the Square Mile.

Other ways to drink and socialise while playing a game include the Dabbers Bingo club and the Fairgame arcade at St Paul’s.

Dabbers brings cabaret and comedy to the traditional game of bingo with eccentric themed nights, and Fairgame is a modern version of the type of arcades you’d typically find at a beachfront, with games like hook-a-duck, Derby horse racing and alley hoop.
