]]> 2467266Adam Bloodworth Adam Bloodworth Clearview AI fights £7.5m UK privacy fine over scraped web photos https://www.cityam.com/clearview-ai-fights-7-5m-uk-privacy-fine-over-scraped-web-photos/ Tue, 20 Oct 2026 14:57:10 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2467081

US tech firm Clearview AI is challenging a UK privacy watchdog ruling that found it breached GDPR rules by collecting and using images of UK residents scraped from the internet and social media. The Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) imposed a £7.5m fine on the US-based tech company in May 2022 and asked it to delete UK residents’ [...]]]>

US tech firm Clearview AI is challenging a UK privacy watchdog ruling that found it breached GDPR rules by collecting and using images of UK residents scraped from the internet and social media.

The Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) imposed a £7.5m fine on the US-based tech company in May 2022 and asked it to delete UK residents’ data after finding it had used images of people in the UK that were collected from social media and the web to create a global online database to be used for facial recognition.

The ICO also ordered the AI company, which builds and sells a database of images used for facial recognition technology primarily for law enforcement and government agencies outside the UK, to stop scraping and using UK residents’ personal data.

Clearview appealed the fine and enforcement notice, bringing legal proceedings to the First-Tier Tribunal in 2023 and arguing the data watchdog lacked power to enforce against a company operating in a different jurisdiction; the court ruled in its favour.

However, in October 2025, the Upper Tribunal overturned the decision after the ICO appealed. The court ruled that the regulator had jurisdiction over the US tech firm and could enforce against it, establishing that Clearview AI obtaining and storing images of UK residents constituted ‘behavioural monitoring’ under the GDPR.

The tech firm was at the Court of Appeal on Tuesday and Wednesday as it sought to overturn the Upper Tribunal ruling and reinstate the First-Tier Tribunal ruling.

Decision may have ‘implications’ for AI firms

Nicola Cain, chief executive and principal consultant at legal consultancy firm Handley Gill, told City AM the decision may have implications for AI companies which carry out similar activities.

“While Clearview AI’s appeal against the £7.5m penalty imposed by the ICO is on a technical point of law relating to whether, as a foreign entity, it is subject to the UK GDPR and required to protect the personal data of individuals in the UK, the principles involved have a wide application, with implications for AI developers, data brokers and database operators who scrape and aggregate personal information from the internet and share it for purposes including AI training.

“Should the ICO prevail in its argument that systematic scraping of online data constitutes behavioural monitoring, the Clearview AI fine may just be the first of many,” Cain added.

An ICO spokesperson said as the hearing “forms part of ongoing legal proceedings in relation to the £7.5m monetary penalty and enforcement notice we issued to Clearview AI Inc. in 2022” it “would not be appropriate for the Information Commission to comment further while the case is before the court.”

Clearview AI was contacted for comment.

Prem Rugby will this week announce Thatchers as a new commercial partner as Elton John’s Rocket Sports agency continues to hunt for league sponsors, City AM understands.

The English top flight counts London Pride as its beer sponsor but will add the West Country brand to its partnership roster as official cider partner.

It is part of a push to expand the commercial portfolio of Prem Rugby after onboarding Rocket Sports, which is owned by Crocodile Rock songsmith John. 

Rocket Sports counts the likes of Sir Jason Kenny and Dame Laura Kenny within its athlete management division.

The firm is in the market on behalf of Prem Rugby to seek sponsors for English rugby union’s top competition. Its title partner, insurance giant Gallagher, currently pays an annual high seven-figure sum having extended its deal with Prem Rugby in 2024.

Thatchers pour into Prem Rugby

The Thatchers deal follows recent sponsorship renewals with ball-maker Gilbert and trading platform Etoro. The likes of Defender, Funding Circle and Buffalo Trace feature within the wider portfolio.

Thatchers already has a presence in the Gallagher Prem, sponsoring West Country duo Bath and Bristol Bears as well as East Midlands side Leicester. It also features as a sponsor of both Sussex and Somerset County Cricket Clubs, as well as Hampshire and the Utilita Bowl, which will host one of England cricket’s Ashes Tests next summer.

The cider brand, based at Myrtle Farm in Somerset, earlier this year posted turnover of £124m for the year to August 2025, with profits touching £17m.

But its Companies House filings warned that “the regulatory and taxation environment is becoming increasingly complex and burdensome”, adding that “upcoming taxes and levies continue to add uncertainty to the financial strain”.

They concluded: “Collectively, these factors make operating within the industry more challenging, increasing costs for producers and ultimately impacting affordability for customers.”

]]> 2467125Matt Hardy Matt Hardy Barclays set for investment bank boost as Venkat’s overhaul in focus https://www.cityam.com/barclays-set-for-investment-bank-boost-as-venkats-overhaul-in-focus/ Tue, 20 Oct 2026 13:53:38 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2467270

Barclays‘ investment bank could be in line for another major boost. But Samuel Norman takes a look at the progress investors will be wanting to hear on its latest strategy plans. When CS Venkatakrishnan laid out his sweeping restructuring of Barclays he promised a “simpler, better and more balanced” bank.  Key to this was reducing [...]]]>

Barclays‘ investment bank could be in line for another major boost. But Samuel Norman takes a look at the progress investors will be wanting to hear on its latest strategy plans.

When CS Venkatakrishnan laid out his sweeping restructuring of Barclays he promised a “simpler, better and more balanced” bank. 

Key to this was reducing reliance on investment banking operations, which had proven to be a volatile source of revenue due to its unpredictability across dealmaking and trading. 

Speaking at the beginning of 2024, Venkat said the investment bank has to be “higher returning” but also become a “smaller part of Barclays”. 

Unfortunately for Venkatakrishnan, known in the industry as Venkat, market tensions have kept the investment bank centre stage across the group – and come Thursday it will be under the spotlight during the group’s third-quarter update.

Last year, the investment bank made up 44 per cent of the group’s revenue, thanks largely to the market chaos triggered by President Donald Trump’s tariff trade offensive. Even while traditional deal advisory lagged, trading desks made hay, with equities income rising 12 per cent to £3.2bn. 

In the first half of 2026, there were new geopolitical tensions, same outcome. Barclays investment banking division saw its income climb 11 per cent year-on-year to £8bn for the first half of the year. 

Equities income soared 45 per cent to £1.3bn in the second quarter alone as traders capitalised on the market swings and volatility drawn out by the Middle East conflict. Investment bank income grew as a share for the group to 48.4 per cent. 

The geopolitical crises may have derailed Venkat’s hopes to make investment banking operations a smaller share of the bank, but his strategy to tighten the balance sheet has worked behind the scenes.

The bank chief made no specific target around revenue share but instead pledged to bring return on tangible equity (RoTE) for the investment bank in line with the wider group. RoTE is a key profitability ratio, measuring a company’s net income relative to the average value of a company’s common equity.

As the Toast the City Awards approaches, we’re looking at some of the cultural highlights in the Square Mile that could take home a coveted Slice of Toast. Today we look at Finalist Dr Johnson’s House and the new Blue Plaque for his brilliant mentee Francis Barber.

Doctor Johnson’s House is a worthy Finalist in our Toast the City Awards. But did you know there is another fascinating cultural figure linked to the site – and that you can visit it right now?

Dr Samuel Johnson will be a name recognisable to many – he was a writer, critic and lexicographer perhaps best known for writing A Dictionary of the English Language in 1755, an incredibly important work that helped define the way the English language was thought of and studied. He resided at what we now call Dr Johnson’s House in Gough Square in Fleet Street Quarter, a Grade I-listed late 17th-century building that he rented for 11 years (it became a museum in 1912).

Dro Johnson’s House was the first landmark in the City of London to be given a Blue Plaque, earning the accolade 150 years ago. Now another Blue Plaque joins it – one dedicated to Francis Barber, Dr Johnson’s servant, friend and heir who would become Britain’s first black school teacher.

The wonderful Francis Barber

Barber, a West African man born into slavery in Jamaica, came to London as a child and lived at Dr Johnson’s house from 1752 to 1756, working there as his servant. Dr Johnson supported him and his family and helped secure his financial future, including making Barber the sole heir and beneficiary of a trust established in his will, something that was sadly controversial at the time.

Dr Johnson’s House is now a charity that runs a museum at the site and is believed to be the only surviving property in the City that was home to a formerly enslaved person who later lived there as a free man.

Of the 140 plaques in the Square Mile, most of them commemorate institutions and organisations, such as the Samaritans, the Great Synagogue and Royal College of Physicians, with only 32 plaques representing individuals. Following a comprehensive review, the scheme has been redesigned to provide a modern, transparent, and inclusive process with clear guidance, embedded equality, equity, diversity and inclusion principles.

While each plaque will be funded primarily by applicants or their sponsors, a new annual City of London Corporation funding pot will support at least one outstanding application each year.

Brendan Barns, chair of the City of London Corporation’s Culture, Heritage and Libraries Committee, said: “Our Blue Plaques Scheme makes a welcome return and highlights the City of London Corporation’s renewed commitment to commemorating remarkable people, places and institutions that have shaped the Square Mile.

“It is our hope that the redesigned scheme will attract thoughtful and persuasively-written applications from a wide range of backgrounds, all of them reminding us that, behind every Blue Plaque is a story worth telling.”

Celine Luppo McDaid, the Hyde director of Dr Johnson’s House, said: “We are thrilled to celebrate the remarkable life of Francis Barber with this Blue Plaque. Enslaved on a Jamaican plantation, Barber came to London and, in this house, he learned to read and write, going on to become the first Black teacher in British history. His story is central to our commitment to bringing long-overlooked lives into the present day.

“As the House of Words, Dr Johnson’s House explores and represents the experiences and legacies of Francis Barber and the extraordinary people who were living here in the middle of the 18th century. By engaging with issues such as friendship, grief, gender, identity, slavery and mental health, the lives of those who went before us resonate with our 21st century audiences.”

Andy Burnham and John Healey have spoken at length about efforts to provide “breathing space” to both households and businesses. This task at next week’s Budget has now become more difficult. 

Over the summer the jobs market continued to weaken. Workers are at risk of being worse off while job seekers are finding it harder to secure new gigs and hiring appetite cools. 

Including bonuses, wage growth continued to slow, falling to 3.7 per cent. When bonuses are excluded, the annualised growth in average weekly earnings remained at the lowest level in six years. 

These earnings are partly satisfactory to the Bank of England, which worries about a spike in wages fuelling higher prices set by firms. Although they remain far lower than public sector pay settlements, private sector earnings growth is at a level consistent with the Bank of England’s target to reach two per cent inflation in the medium term. 

However, what might worry the government more than it does the Monetary Policy Committee is the narrowing growth of wages in real terms. Annual pay growth adjusted for inflation was 0.6 per cent, far lower than the levels of over two per cent seen when Labour was elected into power in mid-2024. 

This pay squeeze is at the nub of the cost of living pressures that Healey is concerned about. 

Thomas Pugh, chief economist at the consulting firm RSM UK said it was “extremely likely” that private sector workers were set to take a “real terms pay cut” in the coming months as inflation rises higher above three per cent. 

“That will intensify the pressure on Burnham and Healey to come up with a package to support the cost of living in the Budget next week,” Pugh said. 

The challenge Healey has, which is not particular to this chancellor, is that he has little room for manoeuvre. His fiscal headroom is projected to have been halved to around £12bn. Healey has ruled out some revenue-raisers in the forms of a capital gains tax hike. A banking tax is expected to be the main new generator of income for the Chancellor. 

Pugh said the “most likely course is a series of temporary measures designed to blunt the worst of the coming rise in utility bills and inflation, without affecting the fiscal headroom in 2029-30”. 

Healey’s unemployment boost

Healey has something to celebrate. The unemployment rate dropped to 4.7 per cent in the the three-month period between June and August. That fell from a rate of 4.9 per cent previously. Some economists in the City had warned that the unemployment rate was on an upward trajectory, rising to as high as 5.7 per cent in the coming months. 

While joblessness levels could yet rise as a result of cost pressures biting business owners, the lower rate in unemployment, coupled with a slight rise in wage growth, could provide some reprieve to the Chancellor. 

“The Chancellor may also have more room for manoeuvre in next week’s Budget than previously feared,” WPI Strategy economist Martin Beck said. 

“Stronger-than-expected growth and inflation-boosted tax receipts could limit the need for significant tax rises, potentially creating scope for targeted measures such as cutting employers’ National Insurance contributions for younger workers.”

Beck added that the UK economy was not in the midst of an “employment crisis” and rather the jobs market was “stuck in the slow lane”. It may be in the government’s powers to get it firing again.

Apple could be forced to slash the fees it charges rival payment providers and loosen its grip on iPhone contactless technology under new proposals unveiled by Britain’s competition watchdog.

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said on Tuesday that Apple’s high fees and restrictive terms were stifling competition, preventing businesses from developing alternatives to Apple Pay.

The watchdog has proposed requiring the US tech giant to open up its near-field communication (NFC) technology, which enables contactless payments, on fairer commercial terms.

It expects access charges to fall substantially, although it stopped short of proposing a fixed price.

“We have heard that high fees, strict terms, and technical restrictions relating to Apple’s contactless technology make it too difficult for challengers to innovate and compete”, said CMA chief executive Sarah Cardell.

“By removing barriers to entry, we can help create the conditions for brilliant British businesses with great ideas to develop new products and services here”.

The move could allow iPhone users to make contactless payments through rival apps rather than relying on Apple Pay, while opening up the technology for digital IDs, travel passes and car keys.

Apple rivals welcome ‘promoting competition’

The fintech and banking industry have welcomed the crackdown from the watchdog expecting it to broaden competition in the contactless payments network.

“The CMA’s direction creates a real opportunity for UK fintechs to compete on an equal footing with Big Tech,” said David Tirado, chief commerical officer at Revolut.

Adam Jackson, chief strategy officer at fintech industry body Innovate Finance, said: “Opening access to these can support competition and further innovation across fintech products including payments”.

Apple introduced a system allowing third-party developers to access its contactless technology in Britain in 2024, but the CMA said no rival wallet-type product had launched through the arrangement.

However, alternative payment services from providers including Paypal and Klarna have launched in the EU following regulatory intervention.

“Digital wallets are becoming an increasingly important way for people to pay, so we welcome the CMA’s focus on promoting effective competition in this area,” a spokesperson for banking trade body UK Finance said.

They added the open access to NFC functionality on Apple’s operating systems would support innovation “reduce reliance on a single wallet provider.”

The watchdog is proposing that Apple support both major international NFC standards, rather than the single approach currently available to UK developers.

It would also require Apple to justify its access charges against principles covering costs, value and fairness, with the CMA expecting fees to be substantially lower than current levels.

An Apple spokesperson said: “We do not believe the CMA should require Apple to adopt an approach with lower privacy and security protections. We will continue to engage constructively to reach an outcome that is in the best interest of our users.”

The Toast the City Awards are mere days away, with the great and good of the Square Mile preparing to descend upon Steel Yard for the party of the year. One of the Finalists is the stunning Barts North Wing – but did you know there is also an incredible place to grab lunch after your visit? Carys Sharkey dives into Restaurant St Barts.

Walk up from St Paul’s, past the shiny ruins of Bank of America and up to the Smithfield circus, where lawyers and financiers spill out of pubs in the shadow of the market. Head past the drinkers on Cloth Fair and down the narrow Bartholomew’s Passage and back round into Bartholomew Close. Then enter through the wide chocolate-brown door underneath a residential block. 

Setting foot inside Restaurant St Barts is one of the most discombobulating experiences I’ve had arriving for dinner. There are quicker ways to get there. I missed a turn and had to loop around, but the added chaos of high-summer Thirsty Thursday in the City made the arrival in this intensely serene restaurant all the more remarkable. 

The space really is something. From the entrance it opens up in a Scandi-style sweep of wood, linens and light. Chairs in the bar area are burnished with sheepskins and the walls are brutal with concrete lit by mounted candles. But as the restaurant unfurls, past the open kitchen with its driftwood ephemera of drying meats, fruits and stacks of fermenting jars, and into the main dining room, the whole space opens onto the medieval church of St Bartholomew the Great, which dates back to 1123. Nowhere mixes past and present quite like the City.

For executive chef and co-founder Johnnie Crowe, the location is a big part of the restaurant’s draw.

“It really feels like an escape from the city,” he tells me. 

“I think experience-led restaurants like ours need to have an element of intrigue and excitement about every aspect of the experience, and the location we have definitely does that.”

St Barts is a Michelin-starred restaurant that only uses British ingredients in its tasting menus. Crowe, who co-founded St Barts in 2022 with Luke Wasserman and Toby Neill, has built a restaurant around his producers. Before Barts, the trio owned Nest in Shoreditch, which this summer was transformed into the much-lauded and much-Instagrammed British bistro Tavern. But St Barts is where Crowe’s dogged devotion to homegrown suppliers pushes him to put out a seriously unique menu. 

“Our suppliers are the main focus of the restaurant. We’ve spent years building up our relationships and researching new and different people who grow, fish and farm. It allows us to do what we do and be 100 per cent British to the core,” he says.

As with all good meals, dinner at St Barts starts with snacks and cocktails. A martini briny with sea fennel rather than olives is paired with beautifully fatty drapes of house-cured coppa (‘gabagool’ in The Sopranos). Next comes a bomb cheese and onion tart, and then a quail liver parfait on a sort of Hobnob that would also make an amazing pudding. As you move into the church-framed dining room, the table is made up to look like a 17th-century still life of summer’s bounty. A nest of quail eggs, sugar snap peas, a block of pork fat, ears of corn, crab shells, a tangle of red currants. 

It’s here in the dining room that the relationship with British producers – and the way it slips and slides between the familiar and unexpected – really shines. 

The first half of the tasting menu features a dish of peas. The peas, grassy, bittersweet and yet perfectly toothsome, are as good as any in the world. It makes sense for Crowe to centre a dish on them. Glistening in a lovage oil – the most medieval of hardy herbs – the peas top a lardo chawanmushi. Peas, pork and plant: this dish feels so rooted in the British larder (that said, it paired amazingly with a Nikolaihof Grüner Veltliner from Austria that tasted like an extinguished sparkler – wine and coffee are, thankfully, exceptions to the rule). 

Later, quail with a bruising mole (a deeply aromatic Mexican sauce) is served on a plate scattered with little picky bits. It’s a fun, slightly kitschy, squirrel plate of exceptional ingredients, including a heart, a big blackberry and a nasturtium leaf. But the star – and one of the best things I’ve eaten all year – is a side of corn. Crowe makes butter from dried corn and then folds things through fresh British corn which has been barbecued on the cob. 

But then a lobster dish totally upended my expectations of British produce. Served in two parts, it starts with a rich nest of Singapore-leaning noodles, and ends with the tail served with quinoa. The real surprise in both was the sansho, a highly floral, zesty Japanese pepper, which makes the sweet richness of lobster zip. Crowe told me it’s grown in Lewes.

“We source it from Namayasai Farm. Ikuyo, who runs the farm, is incredible. We depend on her for so many different products and absolutely love working with her.”

The UK has more niche suppliers and green-fingered enthusiasts than we give credit for. So perhaps the biggest challenge for a restaurant using solely British ingredients is moving with the ebb and flow of the seasons. As we move through autumn and into winter, corn and peas fade to memory. Crowe plays with fermentation and pickling to stretch the seasons. Meat trim is turned to garum, cherry blossoms and elderflowers are suspended in jars, and “Pink Flamingo peas” from Norfolk are transformed into miso.

So it’s perhaps St Barts’ pudding and signature dish that distils Crowe’s cooking ethos so fully. Barley is inoculated with koji and left to ferment and blacken for a couple of months, producing a chocolatey product that’s then blitzed into a roasty, bitter-rich ganache. The barley is also used to make an ice cream, a caramel and a tuile. Out of a single grain Crowe squeezes out one of the tastiest desserts in London. And when paired with the Domaine de Rancy, a bread and butter vin doux naturel, it’s practically unbeatable. 

Leaving the gentle hold of St Barts and returning to the pint-smashed City is an adjustment. I hope to return soon to see what Crowe can make of the colder, shorter days, and to discover more than I thought possible when it comes to homegrown.

The Toast the City Awards are mere days away – we ask if Whitechapel Gallery has what it takes to bring home a coveted Slice of Toast.

The Whitechapel Gallery is one of the undisputed cultural heavyweights of the Square Mile. Having opened in 1901, with a stunning building designed by the architect Charles Harrison Townsend, it was among London’s first publicly funded galleries. Its mission statement was to democratise the often class-locked art world, bringing “the finest art of the world” to the people of the East End.

It was popular from the get-go, with its debut exhibition, Modern Pictures by Living Artists, Pre-Raphaelites and Old Masters, drawing some 260,000 visitors, although legend has it this was in part down to the novelty of seeing electric lighting as much as the appeal of those Old Masters.

This year marked the Whitechapel Gallery’s 125th year, making it a particularly apt time to look back at its triumphs. There is perhaps no 20th century painting more iconic than Picasso’s Guernica, which has been exhibited in the UK just once… at the Whitechapel Gallery in 1939. Other important artists to have been proudly displayed here include Jackson Pollock, with a 1958 exhibition representing his first major British show, Mark Rothko, who also had his first British show here in 1961, and Frida Kahlo, who was displayed here in 1982, years before she became a household name.

The Whitechapel Gallery in the 1970s onwards

The ascendancy continued in the 1970s and 80s, with artistic director Nicholas Serota (who would go on to be artistic director of the Tate) maintaining its reputation as a leading cultural hotspot. In 2007 the gallery embarked upon a two year redevelopment that greatly increased its display space and helped develop its offering as a community hub, creating an archive and reading room.

Its 125th year has seen exhibitions including Joy Gregory: Catching Flies with Honey, which ran from October 2025 into early 2026; Veronica Ryan: Multiple Conversations (1 April-14 June); Backyard Biennial: East (15 July-6 September); and Cecilia Vicuña: Living Threads (7 October-14 February 2027). 

While it has some fearsome competition in the form of the Barbican, Guildhall, the Bank of England Museum and more, Whitechapel Gallery is a clear contender for one of our coveted Slices of Toast at the 2026 Toast the City Awards.

Introduce yourself and Shoe Lane Library

My name is Ovssanna Kalenderian but I’m known as Sona by everyone including our customers. I the manager of Shoe Lane Library, which is part of Barbican & Community Libraries. I’ve been with Shoe Lane Library for 25 of its 44 years.

And Polestar UK Managing Director Matt Galvin has a good idea of who will want it.

“I’d say it’s the thinking man’s Porsche Taycan,” he tells me.

That is a confident statement, but after sampling both flavours of the Polestar 5, I can see why he makes the comparison.

Style and Substance

Developed from the Precept concept with surprisingly few changes, the production car has a slick, aviation-inspired form and is made from bonded aluminium.

The four-door vehicle is light and rigid, and Polestar claims it has torsional rigidity superior to that of a two-seater sports car or supercar. 

But even without all that, I’d still want the low-slung Polestar 5 for its looks alone.

Fortunately, it delivers on all fronts.

Sharp and Capable

I drove the Polestar 5 Dual Motor and Performance versions, and the former isn’t exactly slow.

Indeed, describing it as the more levelheaded of the two doesn’t do it justice.

It is pin-you-to-your-seat quick, yet exquisitely controlled. Point the car towards a sequence of bends, and it slices through them like a laser through frosted glass, with the chassis feeling calm and planted beneath your backside.

The 550kW (737bhp) Dual Motor delivers 812Nm of torque and does the sacred 0-60mph in 3.8 seconds. That’s enough to make overtaking on a British A or B-road almost preposterously easy.

The only slight fly in the ointment for me is the front seats – they feel a little firm.

That is where the Performance version gets interesting. Its more advanced MagneRide adaptive damping gives the 5 a smoother ride, easing the seats’ firmness and making the overall driving experience feel more sumptuous.

Peachy Performance

And yet, the Polestar 5 Performance version borders on beautifully unhinged.

The numbers give you more than a hint of what it’s capable of before you even sit in it. With 650kW (871bhp), 1,015Nm and a 0-60mph time of 3.1 seconds, you already know this car will thoroughly rearrange your corporate priorities.

But those figures don’t fully prepare you for the real-world sensation. The acceleration is so immediate that it makes you grateful for the engineering of the headrests. It doesn’t lack manners, but the Polestar 5 Performance will absolutely hijack the road with the silent, shocking efficiency of a corporate restructuring. 

My colleague discovered this quite amusingly. At one point, when it was my mischievous co-driver’s turn in the hot seat, he deliberately stamped on the accelerator just as I was lifting a peach-flavoured can of water towards my lips. None of it made it into my mouth. Quite a lot went over my face, T-shirt and coat.

Naturally, revenge was required. Later, I planted my size-11 firmly on the go pedal while his reading glasses were perched on top of his head. The burst of speed promptly pushed them behind his neck. Payback, in electric form.  

Is it possible the Performance version has more muscle than the average commute requires? Maybe.

Does it offer a high return on investment in terms of pure, unadulterated, wicked entertainment? No question.

Built for London

For a car expected to navigate London’s chaotic traffic at least some of the time, being largely engineered in the UK means the Polestar 5 also speaks the language of potholes and speed humps.

The Dual Motor has sophisticated BWI passive dampers and internal rebound coil springs, and, as mentioned earlier, the Performance gets MagneRide adaptive dampers. This advanced suspension system can read the road up to 1,000 times a second and react within three milliseconds. The result is excellent body motion control and an optimal response at all speeds.

Braking is handled by Brembo four-piston callipers in combination with lightweight 400mm two-piece discs, while Michelin tyres, designed for the Polestar 5’s chosen wheel combinations ranging from 20 to 22 inches, complete the package.

Galvin reiterates the car has been engineered with British roads specifically in mind.

“It’s been developed here,” he says. “So it handles great.”

Having personally driven the 5 in both forms, I can confirm the engineering hasn’t been squandered on a vehicle designed merely for posing outside a London office.

That said, the grand tourer does posing brilliantly.

Business Lounge on Wheels

The Polestar 5 has another side to its character that could prove particularly significant in London.

Its design delivers a spacious rear seating area by repositioning the header structure behind the passengers’ heads and using a digital rear-view mirror with a virtual rear window, similar to the Polestar 4. 

The back seats can cool, heat, individually recline and massage – and rear passengers can control the four-zone climate system. A nifty ‘foot garage’ within the battery structure also creates extra foot space behind the front chairs, meaning occupants in the back have a more natural seating position. 

But wait, there’s more. The 5 is primarily a four-seater, although if you lift the central armrest, the 2+2 car effectively becomes a five-seater. The Polestar also has 365 litres of rear boot space, while the 62-litre front luggage area is handy for a small bag and charging cable.

The cabin itself is minimalist, with natural-fibre materials, recycled textiles and a massive panoramic glass roof measuring over two metres long.

Up front, the Recaro-developed seats marry a low driving position with decent bolstering – although, as alluded to before, even more cushioning wouldn’t go amiss. They come finished in Charcoal MicroTech, or optional Bridge of Weir Nappa leather in Zinc or Charcoal. 

Between the front seats is a low centre console with a lockable storage compartment, topped with a rotary audio controller for the 14.5-inch portrait touchscreen. The unit runs Polestar’s Android Automotive operating system with Google built in, alongside a nine-inch digital instrument screen and slightly bigger head-up display.

Audio comes via the Polestar High-Performance Audio system with 10 speakers, or you can up the ante with 21 speakers courtesy of Bowers & Wilkins, with 1,680 watts of power. The latter’s fidelity is so clean, you can almost hear the recording engineer sipping his brew.

In other words, the Polestar 5 won’t make you regret your life choices during a two-hour traffic jam on the M11.

From London to Heathrow

London isn’t short on power and might, and as you’ll know by now, nor is this new grand tourer. But if you’re in business in the City, the only number that might truly dictate your sanity is your electric car’s range. 

Therefore, you’ll be pleased to read that the Polestar 5 Dual Motor has an official maximum range of 416 miles on a single charge, while the Performance version offers up to 351 miles.

An 800V electrical architecture enables the Polestar flagship to charge at up to 350kW on an appropriate DC charger. A 10-80% battery refill can take just 22 minutes, and an external indicator on the car’s C-pillar gives a first-glance indication of the 5’s state of charge.

Galvin is relaxed and reassuring about any anxiety over electric range.

“I do 20,000 miles a year, and I can count them on one hand, the number of times I do 300 miles in a day.”

His point is straightforward. For most trips, a 350-plus-mile electric vehicle already offers more than many people need.

So, if your working life revolves around London, Heathrow Airport, and the odd long motorway journey, the Polestar 5’s mix of range and rapid charging is especially relevant.

Prestige and Presence

There is also the image element. I mean, let’s be honest, while standard cars handle your commute, expensive vehicles manage your reputation. Because, in certain parts of London, the whip outside the office can say almost as much as the person inside it. 

Consequently, design matters – and the Polestar 5 certainly has presence.

“I drove it around central London last week,” Galvin tells me.

“If you want to get noticed, this is a car for you.”

He says that while travelling through Hammersmith and Wandsworth, people absorbed in their phones suddenly looked up as the Polestar passed.

“They’d look up and do a double take.”

I know what he means. From every angle, the Polestar 5 looks big-ticket, prestigious and utterly modern. It has the visual presence of a car whose driver has made it in life.

A New Choice

The Polestar 5 Dual Motor Launch edition starts at £89,500, and the Performance Launch edition at £104,900.

That puts the electric grand tourer solidly into the premium automotive arena, and that’s exactly where Polestar wants it.

The company is chasing consumers who’ve already experienced the usual suspects and want something that feels fresher, rarer and more distinctive.

As Galvin puts it, the potential customer may already have had a Taycan or an Audi RS e-tron GT and be pondering what comes next.

“Up until now, there wasn’t really an alternative,” he says. “And now there is the Polestar 5”.

So, the 5 gives London’s top executives a clear advantage. It lets them drive a car that radiates wealth while steering clear of their contemporaries’ vanilla choices.

And if your glasses end up behind your neck or you wind up smelling of peaches, that’s merely the price of progress.

Fifa sponsors including Visa, Coca-Cola and Adidas “cannot afford to be bystanders” while another crisis grips football’s governing body, says a leading sports integrity advisor.

Commercial partners have been conspicuous by their silence since Fifa president Gianni Infantino’s plan to sell stakes in its World Cup business plunged the organisation into civil war more than two months ago.

Infantino has since withdrawn the proposal and pledged to review governance but concerns persist over transparency and the system of patronage that entrenches power in his office.

“I think that they [sponsors] can certainly not afford to be bystanders. Silence is not neutrality,” Emanuel Macedo de Medeiros, CEO of the Sport Integrity Global Alliance, told City AM.

“And have you heard anybody saying anything? No, we haven’t. That is tremendously important, and we have been encouraging sponsors to be part of this united front, this coalition of the willing that Siga represents.”

The current crisis of confidence in Fifa comes little more than a decade after the corruption scandal that tore through the governing body and ousted then-president Sepp Blatter in 2014. 

Back then, Visa, Coca-Cola and Adidas all publicly urged Fifa to reform, while Sony and Castrol chose not to renew their commercial deals. 

‘Fifa needs an antidote not an aspirin’

“Twelve years ago football was hit by the biggest tsunami that has shaken up not just the image and perception and credibility of institutions but the whole cluster,” he said. 

“We all remember the investigations and the front pages, with criminal investigations and trials involving marketing executives, sponsors – not just Fifa, not just football. 

“We see this as a systemic problem, and unless sport acts by putting in place robust regulations, effective accountability and oversight, we will be repeating the same recipe over and over again.”

The Fifa Council last week voted to establish a working group to review Fifa’s governance framework. 

Infantino also apologised for sidelining the council in drawing up plans for the World Cup sell-off but European chiefs Uefa have said that they are still waiting for questions to be answered.

Siga’s recommendation is that any Fifa governance review must be truly independent, wide-ranging, transparent and with provisions for action baked in from the outset.

“We all remember football and sport’s reputation being dragged through the mud,” Medeiros said of the 2014 Fifa scandal, which led to the FBI carry out dawn raids. 

“We had to stop at that, not just with an aspirin but with an antidote that could shield all institutions and individuals for the future, based on a set of universal standards.”

A US cybersecurity startup valued at $3.5bn is opening a new London hub as part of a $200m expansion across Europe, the Middle East and Africa, creating 200 jobs as demand for cyber defences surges.

Chainguard, backed by investors including Sequoia Capital, Lightspeed and General Catalyst, will establish its regional headquarters in Clerkenwell as it expands its engineering, sales and customer support teams.

The investment comes as Britain seeks to attract more overseas tech investment, while a fresh wave of cyber attacks on major retailers has exposed the growing cost of security breaches.

Chainguard, which specialises in securing open-source software, said AI was making it easier for hackers to exploit weaknesses in widely used applications.

“Pulling open source straight from public registries is like picking a USB stick up off the pavement and plugging it into your laptop”, said Ian Burley, the company’s EMEA vice president.

“Maybe you could survive that when finding a flaw took a human engineer months, but you can’t now that a model does it in an afternoon”.

The company said annual recurring revenue across EMEA had risen more than 400 per cent over the past year, while its regional customer base had grown eightfold.

Its new Clerkenwell office will serve as a base for nearly 70 existing UK employees, with the 200 new roles spread across the wider EMEA region.

London attracts fresh tech investment

The expansion follows a string of commitments from US tech giants to Britain’s growing AI and cybersecurity sectors.

Earlier this month, chipmaker Nvidia announced plans to invest in five British startups, alongside a $250m pledge of computing resources for UK AI safety research.

The investment also comes amid renewed concerns over cyber threats to British businesses.

London-listed Asos recently faced threats from hackers claiming to have accessed customer data, while H&M launched an investigation into a suspected breach.

Fashion retailers Hobbs, Whistles and Phase Eight were also affected by a cyber incident at their parent company’s London business.

The attacks follow last year’s breaches at Marks and Spencer, Co-op and Harrods, which exposed the financial cost of disruption to major retailers. Co-op previously said its attack cost £206m in revenue.

Chainguard said its expansion would help companies prevent attacks before hackers could exploit weaknesses in their systems.

The startup now serves more than 800 customers globally, including European businesses Siemens and Aleph Alpha.

As Greek government bonds yield lower interest than France’s, the Eurozone faces a critical test over whether European institutions will enforce fiscal rules consistently or protect politically influential member states, says Tim Focas

If someone had told investors during the eurozone debt crisis of 2012 that Greece would one day borrow more cheaply than France, you would have put them in a straitjacket. Yet here we are at the back end of 2026, and French ten-year government bonds are yielding 4.9 per cent, against Greece’s 4.36 per cent. The country once synonymous with sovereign bankruptcy is now being charged less to borrow than one of the European Union’s founding powers. Welcome everyone, roll up roll up, and look to see the Eurozone’s spectacular see through the looking-glass economy.

But an Alice in Wonderland production this certainly is not. For anyone who was unlucky enough to have lived through the Greek debt crisis, this turning of the tables puts a ginormous elephant in the room and begs the question, when the next sovereign debt crisis does hit Europe, whose interests will the EU really protect?

Investors who still have the scars to prove what happened last time will inevitably be asking themselves this question right now. Back in 2012, Greece completely rearranged its government debt, and imposed a 53.5 per cent nominal reduction in the amount of debt owed on private bondholders. Unfortunately, this only masqueraded over the true destruction of investors’ wealth. The remaining 46.5 per cent wasn’t handed back in cash and much came in the form of long-dated, low-interest bonds worth much less than their face value.

Meanwhile, the Eurosystem’s holdings escaped as Greece retrospectively inserted collective-action clauses into bonds issued under Greek law which allowed most creditors to force restructuring terms upon disgruntled investors. To put it another way, the rules were basically rewritten after investors had bought the bonds. At the same time though, the European Central Bank and national central banks had exchanged their eligible Greek bonds for securities outside the restructuring and, as a result, their holdings were protected while private investors absorbed enormous losses. Then, just to make sure everything was watertight, the European Court of Human Rights subsequently accepted that the restructuring interfered with investors’ property rights, but concluded that the interference was justified by the exceptional circumstances and wider public interest. Legally permissible perhaps, but the question that still lingers to this day is was it really equitable?

Political risk

Unlike Greece though, France is the lifeblood of the EU budget and, alongside Germany, is the cornerstone of political power in Brussels. That makes its precarious borrowing position particularly uncomfortable for those passionate about protecting the Eurozone at all costs. Now let’s not get things twisted, France is certainly not Greece if only because it has a much larger and more liquid debt market. Nevertheless, investors shouldn’t forget that sovereign bonds carry huge political as well as credit risk. Staunch ECB’s defenders will of course make the case that protecting central-bank holdings was imperative to prevent financial contagion.

Nobody would dispute this, but at the same time, it doesn’t erase the losses imposed on private creditors. If France’s public finances get worse, would financial institutions across the bloc really tolerate a Greek-style treatment of creditors? Or would we suddenly see a more “flexible” interpretation of Europe’s precious rules-based system when the country that just so happens to have its fiscal feet to the fire is too politically important to make an example out of?

That is the double-standards predicament confronting Europe, which they have no choice but to face head on once again. And, if this wasn’t uncomfortable enough, the yield advantage offered by French bonds over Greek bonds is currently not even one full percentage point. Would any investor in their right mind accept a modest premium of 0.36 per cent in return for all the political uncertainty? With many still licking their wounds from how quickly contractual protections can be overwhelmed by sovereign necessity, surely they would have to think very carefully.

Pricing inflation, interest rates and assessing default probabilities is just what markets naturally do. However, pricing in the likelihood of European institutions tweaking the rules when it politically suits doesn’t come as naturally to investors as Greece taught them at extraordinary cost. With France now firmly in the firing line, we may soon find out whether Europe has learned its lesson.

Tim Focas is head of capital markets at Aspectus Group

Technical universities in partnership with employers like Dyson can help up-skill the population, re-industrialise the nation and solve the NEETSs crisis. And Hereford is already showing the way forward, says Byron Evans

A million young people are not in education, employment or training (NEET). Over 250,000 vacancies sit unfilled because the skilled workers needed are unavailable. Competition for graduate roles has reached a historic high, with firms receiving an average of 140 applications per graduate vacancy – up from 86 in 2022/23. It is ironic that England has more universities than ever, yet employers are crying out for technical skills. A new Policy Exchange report, Engineered for Success, endorsed by Sir James Dyson and Lord Blunkett, argues the answer lies in a new wave of technical universities.

A consensus is beginning to emerge across the political spectrum that the current higher education settlement is not delivering effectively. Burnham wants to value the hard hat as much as the graduation cap, and the Conservatives have pledged to double the apprenticeship budget. The British public have noticed the fall from grace: the proportion of people who believe a degree is not worth the time, and money, has jumped from 14 per cent in 2005 to 34 per cent in 2025.

Skill-shortage vacancies now constitute 27 per cent of all vacancies and are concentrated most acutely in key technical sectors like construction (45 per cent) and manufacturing (34 per cent). At the same time, England has the most over-qualified workforce in the OECD’s adult skills survey, at 37 per cent. A lack of traditional, three-year bachelor’s degrees is clearly not the problem: around 130,000 young NEETs already hold a higher education qualification.

The frozen fee, has instead incentivised provision of cheaper, classroom-based subjects, at the expense of lab-based courses. Between 2012/13 and 2024/25, enrolments in business and management rose by 71 per cent, while engineering and technology grew by just 10 per cent.

Our skew away from skilled trades is out of kilter compared to similarly developed economies; in 2023, engineering, manufacturing and construction accounted for just 8.9 per cent of UK first-degree graduates – against 33 per cent in China and 25 per cent in Germany. This scarcity is duly reflected in the labour market – UK STEM graduates earning 18 per cent more than the average wage – nearly double Germany’s 10 per cent equivalent.

Hereford shows the way

There is an alternative to the current model. In Hereford, the New Model Institute for Technology and Engineering (NMITE) has designed its curriculum with more than 80 employers, including BAE Systems and Balfour Beatty. Students work in a different environment to a traditional university, with a nine-to-five workday, on tasks set by these employers directly. NMITE offers expedited degrees, completing a masters in three years rather than four, leaving with £12,060 less debt and entering the workforce a year earlier. Many of its first graduates went straight into competitive engineering roles at an average starting salary of £35,000.

Policy Exchange has mapped 57 English towns of 60,000 people or more with no university of their own, home to 5.5m people, to identify the best locations for new NMITE-type institutions. The top ten strongest cases for an NMITE, led by Hartlepool, Grimsby and Barnsley, are all in the North.

Policy Exchange has long argued that technical routes deserve parity of esteem with academic ones. Our 2025 report, From School to the Skilled Workforce, advocated for University Technical Colleges, 14-19 schools with an explicit focus on technical pathways. NMITE-type institutions are the next rung on that ladder.

The current regulatory landscape makes establishing such institutions unduly arduous. We argue the process should be made easier, with a £50m Seed Development Fund, greater powers for mayors to establish their own institutions, working with private partners, and an expedited registration process for NMITE-type institutions.

A roll-out of NMITE-type universities offers much-needed diversity in degree-level provision – and could provide the bedrock of technical skills required for any serious re-industrialisation of Britain.

Byron Evans is a research fellow at Policy Exchange and co-author of ‘Engineered for Success’.

Most people protect their digital lives with a handful of passwords they've memorized—a security practice so common it's become catastrophic.]]>

For about five months, a browser extension sat quietly on the home computers of 154 people and watched them log in.

The researchers never saw a password. Everything was hashed on the machine before it went anywhere, leaving them with the shape of each one: its length, its mix of characters, the site it was typed into, and whether the same string had appeared before.

Very often, it had.

What 154 people actually typed

Sarah Pearman and her co-authors at Carnegie Mellon University presented the results at a 2017 computer security conference, having followed each participant for an average of 147 days. Those people logged in across 26 web domains apiece and covered the lot with fewer than 10 distinct passwords.

Roughly 60 per cent of those distinct passwords were recycled, either typed identically on another site or built around a chunk of four or more characters lifted from one the same person used elsewhere.

Banking got no special treatment. Around 85 per cent of the passwords on financial sites appeared elsewhere too, and nearly all of that crossover ran into unrelated categories, so the login for a savings account was also the login for a shoe shop.

What partial reuse looks like up close

Mostly it looks like adding a character.

Among passwords that shared a substring with another, the most common gap between the two was a single character. Digits were the strongest predictor in the Carnegie Mellon model, multiplying the odds of reuse by more than twelve. The authors’ own explanation is that a password with a number in it satisfies more websites’ fussy signup rules, so it travels further.

The tidy minority had barely any accounts

Ten participants mostly built something new for each site, which sounds like a win for good habits until you look at what they were doing online. With one exception, every one of them entered passwords on eight domains or fewer, and they were active on their computers on only 17 per cent of the days they spent enrolled.

The heavy users went the other way. Ninety-four participants, the largest cluster by far, both copied passwords outright and modified them, and they averaged 32 online accounts each. Discipline held up fine at eight accounts and collapsed at thirty.

The password manager result, with a handbrake

Only 19 of the 154 participants had a password manager installed, and the study found no measurable effect on either reuse or strength.

That result deserves caution. One paper is one paper, the subgroup is tiny, and the software could not tell whether people were generating random strings or merely parking passwords they had invented themselves. Rick Wash and colleagues at Michigan State University, who watched 134 participants over six weeks, found each password being reused on 1.7 to 3.4 websites. Their study did not measure partial reuse at all, so the higher figure out of Pittsburgh partly reflects counting a habit nobody had counted before.

Why a recycled password is worth money

Somewhere there is a text file with an old forum password in it, sitting in a folder alongside a few hundred million others. Troy Hunt, the Australian security researcher behind the breach notification service Have I Been Pwned, has documented the trade in combo lists, which are exactly that: vast dumps of email and password pairs scraped out of past breaches. Cheap automated tools fire them at unrelated websites until one opens. Defending against it is awkward, because a successful run looks identical to a customer logging in correctly.

One shared string, and the breach at a defunct hobby forum becomes a problem at an email provider.

The rules that encouraged this have been withdrawn

In 2025, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology finalised revision 4 of its digital identity guidelines, and the password section reads like a quiet apology. Websites must stop demanding mixtures of character types, and they must stop forcing periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise. Password managers and autofill have to be allowed, and every new password gets checked against blocklists of strings already known to have leaked.

Each of those requirements targets the behaviour the extension recorded: a handful of memorable strings, nudged sideways by a digit, stretched across an entire online life.

The standard now assumes a machine is doing the remembering. Anyone who ever stuck a “1” on the end to get past a signup form was just covering the shift until it arrived.

]]> A telemarketer refused to keep his webcam on for nine hours a day while working from home and was fired the next day — a Dutch court ruled the demand invaded his privacy and ordered his employer to pay him roughly €75,000 https://siliconcanals.com/d-a-telemarketer-refused-to-keep-his-webcam-on-for-nine-hours-a-day-while-working-from-home-and-was-fired-the-next-day-a-dutch-court-ruled-the-demand-invaded-his-privacy-and-ordered-his-employ/ Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:15:27 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109737

A Dutch court sided with a worker who refused constant video surveillance, forcing his employer to pay damages—a warning shot across the evolving battle over remote work monitoring.]]>

A camera that stayed switched off cost a Florida software company about 75,000 euros.

It belonged to a telemarketer working from the small Dutch town of Diessen, employed since January 2019 by Chetu, an American software firm that at the time ran a Dutch office in Rijswijk. On 23 August 2022 he was told to join something called the Corrective Action Program, which meant staying logged in for his whole shift, sharing his screen and leaving his laptop camera on. He shared the screen. The camera stayed dark.

His objection was brief and entirely unlegalistic. Court filings quoted by The Register record him saying he was not comfortable being monitored for nine hours a day, calling it “an invasion of my privacy” and noting that his laptop activity was already visible to management.

Two more instructions followed, each firmer than the last. On 26 August he was dismissed on the spot, the stated reasons being refusal to work and insubordination.

Three days from the first instruction to the sack.

What the company argued

Chetu’s case, set out in the published judgment of the Court of Zeeland-West-Brabant, was that watching a remote worker through a webcam is no different from a manager walking past a desk. Performance software already sat on the man’s laptop, and that was not considered enough. Chetu wanted to see him working.

Nobody from the company turned up to make the argument in person, as TechCrunch noted, so it went undefended.

What the judge decided

Ruling on 28 September 2022, the subdistrict judge in Tilburg found that ordering an employee to keep a camera running for a full shift conflicted with his right to respect for private life, and that nothing had been offered to justify it. An unreasonable instruction cannot be unreasonably refused, so there had been no refusal to work and no grounds for summary dismissal.

Data protection law dropped out early. On the understanding that no footage would be recorded, stored or used for anything, the judge treated the monitoring as falling outside data processing altogether, and tested it directly against Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alongside Strasbourg case law holding that filming staff at work, covert or not, is a serious intrusion into private life. Had the images been kept, the analysis would have looked quite different.

One much-quoted line deserves care. Coverage including a report in Fortune presented the claim that all-day camera tracking is disproportionate and not allowed in the Netherlands as a finding of the court. In the Dutch record it sits among the employee’s own submissions. What the judge actually held was narrower, and sufficient: this instruction, to this man, in his own home, breached Article 8 with no justification advanced.

Why the sum was so large

Almost none of the money was a penalty for the privacy breach. The largest slice, 50,000 euros, was a billijke vergoeding, an equitable award Dutch judges reserve for employers whose conduct in ending a job has been seriously culpable, with a wrongful summary dismissal among the standard triggers, as the Amsterdam employment firm Workx Advocaten explains. A Dutch judge has now looked at that question once, and the employer left lighter.

Estonia’s population stood at 1,360,745 at the start of 2026, according to Statistics Estonia. That is smaller than many single cities. Out of it has come ten companies that reached a billion-dollar valuation at some point in their history, among them Skype, Wise, Bolt, Pipedrive, Playtech and Veriff, according to Invest in Estonia’s own tally.

Using CB Insights’ underlying company data alongside that population figure, a figure Invest in Estonia and outlets including Fintech Baltic put at roughly 7.1 unicorns per million residents, based on Invest in Estonia’s cumulative count of companies that have ever reached $1B — not a live ranking CB Insights itself publishes, second only to Liechtenstein and more than three times the United States’ rate of about 2.2 per million.

The tiger leap that came before the unicorns

This density didn’t happen by accident, and it didn’t start with a startup. In 1996, five years after regaining independence from the Soviet Union, Estonia launched a state programme called Tiigrihüpe, or Tiger Leap, championed by future president Toomas Hendrik Ilves and education minister Jaak Aaviksoo. It wasn’t only talent that recirculated. Toivo Annus, one of Skype’s founding engineers who led its engineering team until the eBay sale, went on to co-found Ambient Sound Investments with three other early Skype engineers in 2003, a private investment firm that has since backed more than 50 early-stage ventures, according to documented accounts of his career. The ecosystem underneath those ten companies is larger and more active than the unicorn count alone suggests. A per-capita unicorn count says nothing about how many of those companies are still worth a billion dollars today, still headquartered in Estonia, or profitable. Playtech moved its primary listing to London years ago. Skype no longer trades as an independent business at all. For a country with fewer people than a mid-sized American county, that is the more durable claim.

An hour disappears into the phone and the honest inventory afterwards runs to three items: a man cutting marble, somebody’s strong opinion about interest rates, a dog on a skateboard.

None of it is retained in any way worth having. The hour still lands like work.

That mismatch, between the feeling of effort and the absence of anything learned, has a reasonable research explanation behind it, and willpower barely features in it.

A feed is a run of cold starts

Reading a book is one long continuous job. The brain loads a setting, a cast, an argument, and then keeps using that same setup for as long as the reading lasts.

A feed offers nothing of the kind.

Each post arrives with its own subject, tone, format and rules, which means the machinery of attention has to reconfigure itself before any of the content can be processed.

A feed adds another recurring job: a verdict. Each item has to be sized up for whether it is true, whether it is funny, whether it is aimed at anyone in particular. That call gets made before the thing can be dismissed, and then made again at the next one, and the one after that.

Psychologists have taken that reconfiguration apart. In a paper published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, Joshua Rubinstein, David Meyer and Jeffrey Evans described two stages: goal shifting, meaning the decision to do this now instead of that, and rule activation, meaning the swap of mental instructions from the old job to the new one. Both stages take time. A single switch might cost only a few tenths of a second. That sounds trivial until you count the switches inside an hour of scrolling.

Their experiments used arithmetic and shape-sorting rather than phones, so applying the finding to a feed is an inference, not a measurement.

Switching also leaves something on the floor.
